subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: U.S.-CANADA  ANNOUNCEMENT OF JOINT MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE ON DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to table an exchange of notes between the Canadian and United States governments concerning the establishment of a Canada-United States committee on joint defence. Hon. members will recall that the Prime Minister informed the house on July 11 of the agreement reached in the course of the visit of the President of the United States to Canada to establish a joint ministerial committee with authority to consider all matters bearing on the common defence of the North American continent. The exchange of notes which I am tabling today simply records the formal agreement of the two governments in this matter.
The decision of the two governments to establish such a joint ministerial committee stemmed from the recognition by both governments of the need to supplement existing channels of consultation in the defence field. It is intended that the committee will give periodic consideration not only to the military aspects of our common defence but also to the political and economic factors bearing on defence problems.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REPORTED SALE OF MILITARY AIRCRAFT TO U.S. FIRM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure to which minister I should address this question. Perhaps in the circumstances I might address it to the Prime Minister. I regret not having been able to give him notice but the matter was just brought to my attention. It arises out of a Canadian Press dispatch of September 4 to this effect:
Two Mustang fighters were flown out of Calgary yesterday as the vanguard of nearly 100 Canadian fighter planes which have been disarmed and sold to a New York group. . . . The planes have been sold by Crown Assets Corporation to J. H. DeFuria and F. J. Ritts of De Witt, N.Y., for an undisclosed sum. Included in the purchase are more than 40 Sea Furies only recently taken out of active Royal Canadian Navy service. Eventual destination of the planes is being kept secret.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether in fact this sale of 100 planes has been made and what steps have been taken to ensure that these planes do not reach an undesirable destination.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: REPORTED SALE OF MILITARY AIRCRAFT TO U.S. FIRM

With respect to the latter part of the statement, I may say that every course will be followed to assure that the undesirable end to which the hon. member has made reference will be prevented.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT ON USE OF FORCE BY U.S.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT ON USE OF FORCE BY U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a session-ending question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In view of the statement issued by President Eisenhower and Secretary of State Foster Dulles warning the government of China that the United States may use military force, including possible bombing of the Chinese mainland, if necessary to protect the islands it considers essential to the defence of Formosa; and in view of the minister's assurances on August 25 and

Inquiries of the Ministry August 30 that the Canadian government has made no commitment to become involved in the dispute between the communist government of China and the Chinese nationals on the offshore islands, can the minister indicate how unilateral action on the part of the United States government would affect Canada and its arrangements under the NORAD agreement? Can the minister inform the house whether the government has made representations to both parties in this dispute? Has the minister any information he can give to the house with respect to developments in this most disturbing situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Sidney E. Smith (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT ON USE OF FORCE BY U.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I came into the house I received a copy of the question which the hon. member has now addressed to me. I would observe that the hon. member is seized of the situation and that he is quite correct in using the word "may", that the United States "may" use military force.
Coming to the question "can the minister indicate how unilateral action on the part of the United States government would affect Canada", may I say that I stated in the house, as the hon. member observed, on August 25 and 30 that we have made no commitment in respect of any dispute or conflict in the Taiwan straits. In addition to that, I would say that unilateral action on the part of the United States would not involve Canada in any possible conflict in that area.
With respect to the second part of the question I point out to the house that under the earlier co-ordinated air defence scheme in North America as well as under NORAD, our air force defence squadrons would be called upon to defend Canada against an attack on Canada by hostile aircraft.
With respect to the third question, I can tell the house that I have no information to give about the situation in the Formosa straits in addition to what has appeared in the newspapers. I can assure the house that we are keeping in close touch with the various capitals with respect to this situation.

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT ON USE OF FORCE BY U.S.
speechtext: If I may, I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs a supplementary question because of this grave emergency and great danger to world peace. Will Canada consider making representations to both nations in opposition to any acts that might result in a global war?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT ON USE OF FORCE BY U.S.
speechtext:
May I ask
for an elaboration of that question, Mr. Speaker. What does the hon. member mean by "both nations"?

subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT ON USE OF FORCE BY U.S.
speechtext: By "both nations" I mean the United States and red China.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENT ON USE OF FORCE BY U.S.
speechtext: In reply to that question I would say that, as is well known in the house, we have no representation in red China. With respect to the United States, we have made our position very clear and we share with that country, and this has been explicitly expressed, their grave concern about the situation and the appreciation of the great need for restraint.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED MOUNTED POLICE SECURITY GUARD IN WEST BLOCK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Public Works. Can the minister inform the house as to why a most unusual procedure is followed, in that after six o'clock in the evening a member of the R.C.M.P. acts as security guard inside a government building on parliament hill, namely the west block? Why do employees of the House of Commons and Senate whose offices have been there for many years now have to sign: in and sign out after six o'clock, though engaged in the work of the Senate and the House of Commons? Why, sir, do members of the House of Commons, keeping an appointment after six o'clock in the west block, have to be interrogated by the R.C.M.P. as to their business there, and sign in on the entry book before they are allowed to keep an appointment? This happened to me, sir, last night.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minisier of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: REPORTED MOUNTED POLICE SECURITY GUARD IN WEST BLOCK

subtopic: REPORTED MOUNTED POLICE SECURITY GUARD IN WEST BLOCK
speechtext: I understood that all the buildings came under the Department of Public Works. I think, sir, that indirectly the matter of security and the employees of parliament comes under you, Mr. Speaker. the security guard before I am able to answer. I shall do that right away and let the hon. member know.

subtopic: REPORTED MOUNTED POLICE SECURITY GUARD IN WEST BLOCK

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED MOUNTED POLICE SECURITY GUARD IN WEST BLOCK

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police are not in charge of security inside the centre block where the houses of parliament actually meet, but it is my understanding that for some time the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have been in charge of security in the other buildings, that is the east and west blocks. I know that ever since I have been here I have been accustomed to seeing a mounted police constable at the door of the east block.

subtopic: REPORTED MOUNTED POLICE SECURITY GUARD IN WEST BLOCK

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED MOUNTED POLICE SECURITY GUARD IN WEST BLOCK
speechtext: The constable stands inside. The security staff or the protective staff of parliament operate only in the centre block, to my knowledge, and the security arrangements for the other buildings are not under the control of the protective staff of the house or the Senate.

subtopic: REPORTED MOUNTED POLICE SECURITY GUARD IN WEST BLOCK
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might have your indulgence to mention one fact. There seems to be some confusion about what the particular point is. The point concerns the House of Commons administration. Hon. members know that part of the west block was set aside for the use of the House of Commons staff, and it is the interference with the work of the House of Commons staff and the members in the performance of their duties that is at issue, as I understand it. This is quite a different thing from the point raised by the Minister of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED MOUNTED POLICE SECURITY GUARD IN WEST BLOCK
speechtext: Not at all; the point raised by the Minister of Justice was that, as I understood it, for some years the east and west blocks have been using the security services of the R.C.M.P. To my knowledge there has never been previous objection to that. If hon. members find that questioning by the R.C.M.P. in the west block is not acceptable, then I think-

subtopic: REPORTED MOUNTED POLICE SECURITY GUARD IN WEST BLOCK

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

If the hon. member would permit me to complete the answer, I have just pointed out that this is the first time, to my knowledge, that the point has been raised or that anyone has found it objectionable. I was going on to say that if that is the case-if there is objection-then it seems to
Inquiries of the Ministry me I might have a discussion with His Honour, Mr. Speaker, about the matter and perhaps with the leaders of the parties to see if the present system is satisfactory or whether some other system might be worked out in so far as that portion of the west block is concerned which is assigned to the House of Commons staff.

subtopic: REPORTED MOUNTED POLICE SECURITY GUARD IN WEST BLOCK

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister) moved
subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
for leave to introduce Bill No. C-60, for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
He said: Mr. Speaker, because of the circumstances which have arisen, the lateness of the session and the desire of hon. gentlemen to have this matter given the fullest possible consideration, I propose on this occasion simply to follow the course that was

taken in the first session of 1957 by the then prime minister, Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, and I shall refer to the bill in some detail, with the permission of the house.
Thereafter views will be expressed by the Leader of the Opposition and by the hon. member for Assiniboia as the leader of his group and this measure will then remain until next session, to be introduced at the earliest possible date after full representations have been received from those organizations and individuals in our country whose interest over the years has been directed to the necessity for a bill of human rights and fundamental freedoms in our country.
I would be less than frank if I did not say that in introducing this bill I do so following years of endeavour in this regard, years of representations in which were joined others who were then in the house and by two such members in particular, Mr. M. J. Cold-well and Mr. Croll, who is now a member of the other place. I believe the introduction of this measure marks an important day for all Canadians, since it represents the attainment of a goal to which many had looked forward. It is a measure with respect to which, from 1942 onward, I have spoken in this house from time to time, and in support of which I have moved resolutions on a number of occasions.
To draft such a bill has been difficult. The desire has been to keep it strictly within the constitutional powers of the federal parliament. Its aim and purpose has been to give to parliament the opportunity of removing any future danger to the fundamental freedoms of our country, danger which has not been unapparent in the past.
The aim has also been to clothe this bill in simple language. I know there will be criticism of it in that regard, but I would point out that from the earliest biblical times those charters of freedom which have taken their places as landmarks in man's march to liberty, including the Gettysburg speech, were declarations of the rights of man phrased in vital but simple words; for, sir, human rights and fundamental freedoms require no grandiloquent words to contribute to their greatness and importance.
Today what I shall do is underline some of the steps that have been taken during the years in the advocacy of the need of a bill of rights, the necessity for a bill of rights, and the terms. Then I should like to refer to one or two matters for the purpose of assuring that the record in this regard be kept clear, to answer questions that will naturally arise such as why was a constitutional amendment not asked for rather than embodying those rights in a statute; what will happen to the other freedoms that are part and parcel of
Human Rights
our constitutional rights which are not specifically included; what are the provisions in this bill that will assure the maintenance of the security of Canadians in the event of war or other similar national disasters?
This bill of rights and its form represent action to be taken by parliament to carry out one of the major principles of the charter of the United Nations which was designed to assure international co-operation and to ask for the promotion and encouragement of respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, sex, language or religion.
I said this represented the first step toward the achievement of what has been in the minds of Canadian people for many years. Indeed, two petitions were brought to parliament during the years 1947 and 1948, signed by 500,000 in one case and by more than
700,000	in the other, asking for legislation to assure the maintenance of fundamental freedoms in the federal jurisdiction. To that end two committees of parliament were set up which dealt at very great length with the issues, the needs as well as the suggested draftsmanship.
I would like to refer to the divisions of this bill. It consists of two parts, the first being the bill of rights as such. It makes very clear that this bill is entirely within the legislative jurisdiction of parliament. It states:
It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have always existed and shall continue to exist the following human rights and fundamental freedoms-
May I paraphrase those freedoms. They are the right of the individual to life, liberty, security of the person and enjoyment of property, and the right not to be deprived thereof except by due process of law; the right of the individual to protection of the law without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex; freedom of religion; freedom of speech; freedom of assembly and association; and freedom of the press.
I would point out that radio as such or broadcasting in general is not included, because freedom of the press has been defined as including freedom respecting broadcasting. Then in order to make doubly sure that there shall never be a challenge in the future there is provision which states that all the acts of the parliament of Canada enacted before or after the commencement of this portion of the bill and all orders, rules, regulations and laws in effect in Canada or in any part of Canada at the commencement of this part which are subject to be repealed, abolished or altered by the parliament of Canada, shall

Human Rights
be construed and applied so as not to abrogate, abridge or infringe any rights of human freedom.
Then as to the rights of the individual; the right not to be subject to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment; to be deprived of one's rights; to be informed as to the reason for his arrest; of his right to retain and instruct counsel; also the right not to be deprived of any right except after a fair hearing in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice; the right of an individual to a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal for the determination of any criminal charge.
Then in so far as habeas corpus is concerned no one shall be deprived of the remedy by way of habeas corpus for the determination of the validity of his detention or his release if the detention is not lawful.
Then, sir, because of the fact that the United States and many other jurisdictions have adopted bills of rights since the United States did so by the first amendment to the constitution, so as to assure that other fundamental freedoms which are not specifically designated shall not by reason of their absence be considered to be non-existent there is a provision in part II which says:
Nothing in part I shall be construed to abrogate or abridge any human right or iundamental freedom not enumerated therein that may have existed in Canada at the commencement of this act.
This section is placed in the bill to meet the situation to which I have already made reference. A similar section was recommended by the committee of parliament presided over by Senator Roebuck as necessary to meet the situation to which I have just referred.
Then during time of war provision is made, in keeping with the experience of the United States and also the practice and procedure in the United Kingdom, that in so far as the War Measures Act is concerned the effective sections in question, 3, 4 and 5, shall come into force only upon proclamation of the governor in council declaring that war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended, exists. Then in order to maintain the supremacy of parliament, provision is made that the proclamation declaring that war, invasion or insurrection, real or apprehended, exists shall be laid before parliament forthwith after its issue or, if parliament is not sitting, within the first 15 days thereafter.
In other words, while experience has shown both in the United Kingdom and in the United States that in time of war rights on occasion have to be placed in pawn as security for victory, that decision hereafter must be made not by the governor in council but by parliament, thereby restoring to the representatives

of the people the right to declare whether or not, for a period to be designated during the progress of war or an international catastrophe similar thereto, any rights shall be deprived except in consequence of the act of parliament.
I mentioned a moment ago that I would refer to the need for a bill of rights, for there are those who say there is no need. I read recently that the Leader of the Opposition had taken the stand that there was no need. Well, I point out that all across this nation, as a result of experiences which I raise not for the purpose of controversy but simply as a requisite in order to ascertain whether there is a need, there has been a widespread demand for action of this kind in order to preserve and maintain rights against the invasion of an all-powerful state, and I refer at all times to the federal government and federal parliament.
The Canadian constitution, it is said, grants us those rights. Well, our constitution is largely made up of the British North America Act although there are traditions, liberties and prior statutes that are part and parcel thereof as well as that unwritten heritage which is ours. Under the British North America Act it is stated that the Canadian constitution is similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom, but in the experience of the past it has been shown that this declaration does not in any way preserve and maintain fundamental freedoms or those civil liberties and human rights that should be binding on the parliament of Canada. I have here "Charters of our Freedom" prepared by the late Professor Trotter, in which he defines the question of civil liberties in these words:
Civil liberty, or liberty of the person, means one's opportunity to live his own life free from arbitrary or illegal interference by government, or by other persons, with his movement, conduct and opinion. Enjoyment of such freedom by the members of a community can never be complete, for the very laws that safeguard the individual's liberties can do so only by placing restrictions on all persons to prevent them from conduct harmful to one another. Law guards the liberties of each of us by limiting the liberty of all. It must restrain even the rulers themselves In the exercise of their authority over their subjects.
There are many who contend that we do not need a bill of rights because parliament has in the past and can be trusted for the future to safeguard our rights and freedoms. But, sir, unfortunately that has not been the experience. The United States found it necessary to provide for a bill of rights after the constitution had been determined because immediately it became apparent that while fundamental freedoms were generally accepted as being part of the tradition and heritage of the United States and the original colonies, there were such invasions as made

action necessary. Thomas Jefferson contended that it was far better and was the only safe course to have safeguards for personal freedom on the statute books than to trust to the discretion and whims of a majority.
History also reveals that few governments with large majorities want at any time to have their power restricted. I expressed that view sitting on the other side of the house on March 24, 1952. I repeat it today because then I was in a small opposition and today I am on the government side of the house with no small membership. Experience has shown that freedom is not always safe in the custody of an overwhelmingly powerful government supported by an overwhelming majority. Large parliamentary majorities do not always ensure omnicompetence in the preservation of freedom.
I want to refer to several examples in this regard, not for the purpose of bringing up the past but simply to provide enlightenment for the future. In December, 1945, some months after hostilities had ceased and without reference to parliament, three orders in council were passed and declared to be valid by the judicial committee of the privy council, which would have exiled to Japan some
7,000	people of Japanese origin, a large proportion of whom were Canadian citizens. The fact that the privy council said that this could be done, that it was lawful, following the end of hostilities indicates the need of some restraining influence and the declaration of some principle to assure that there shall not be repetition in the future.
On October 4, 1945 an order in council was passed which swept aside habeas corpus, which denied the right of an individual to counsel. Whatever the merits may have been of the action taken, events then and subsequently established that an invasion such as that of a primary fundamental right can be made by the parliament of Canada or under order in council.
As a further example I might cite the Foreign Exchange Control Act. Provision was made under that act that anyone who in the opinion of an official had broken the law, whether or not there was any justification, however illegally he was treated, had no right of recourse to the courts. Finally that was changed. It started under order in council, strong objection was raised here in the House of Commons, and a change was made in the law, Mr. Speaker, to provide that if illegal actions were taken under this act the individual had a right of recourse to the courts; but whatever his loss, whether it amounted to $10,000 or more, the amount
Human Rights
he could recover in the courts in the event of his success was nominal damages of $1 and no costs.
Now, these are just examples. I am not covering the ground, but I am laying the basis for an argument that there is a need. There was an order in council passed setting up a committee to investigate Eldorado. The commission had the power to examine, legally or illegally, lawfully or unlawfully, and to deny an individual who was charged or examined the right of counsel, at the same time denying any right of appeal. Unless restrained, Mr. Speaker, the pathways of power lead to the degradation of the rights of individuals. We are all human and Lord Acton's famous aphorism, sometimes misquoted, that absolute power corrupts absolutely is true whatever your party affiliations may be.
Then in December, 1945, there was introduced the transitional powers bill, subsequently withdrawn but none the less within the power of parliament, whereby the cabinet was asking, by order in council, for the complete control of property in Canada; the forfeiting of property at its will; the control of transportation by railway, water, road and air; and control over business in Canada. Subsequently alterations were made in that bill. It was withdrawn and a new bill was substituted, but those are indications of what will happen when you have a powerful parliament unless there is an overriding declaration to preserve the rights of the individual.
I can think of another example, and I opposed this but I am not saying the stand was correct. I am not here to judge. Legislation was introduced in April, 1946, which provided that from then on no transportation company in Canada could operate civil air lines. This legislation went through, but later on it became inconvenient. There was not an order in council passed, but there was a minute of council passed that operation of the statute, which had become law, should be postponed.
I might cite another example. Again I say I am mentioning these cases merely as a basis for answering those who say that a bill of rights is not necessary. In 1946, a Mr. Oatman started an action against the wheat board for certain rights which he claimed. The case came finally before the court of appeal of Manitoba. He was then in a position to launch an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. I do not know what the merits of the case were, whether he was right or wrong, but he was a Canadian who had the right of appeal to the courts. An order in council was passed denying him the right to appeal to the supreme

Human Rights
court; indeed, it denied anybody else the right to commence a similar action, or to continue an action which he had legally started.
There are many other cases here before me, but I shall not make reference to them now. They do support the stand taken by the Canadian Daily Newspapers Association, representative of 97 per cent of the English and French newspapers of Canada, that experience of the past had shown that a bill of rights was necessary and ought to be brought into being. Bruce Hutchison, writing in 1947 between May 30 and June 3, used these words:
-the people and parliament of Canada are beginning to think that safeguards are necessary because, in recent times, basic human liberties have been infringed in this country.
He said at another time in the same series of articles:
Thus, after assuming for 80 years that liberty was safe in Canada without any sure legal guarantee, parliament has been compelled to realize that liberty has lately been infringed by the state in a fashion unforeseen by the framers of our constitution. The infringement as yet is small, but it can grow. The purpose of a bill of rights is to make sure that it does not grow.
I have here as well the views of one who, like Mr. Hutchison, has not been known as a supporter of the party to which I belong. I refer to Professor A. R. M. Lower of Queen's University. In an article entitled "Some reflections on a Bill of Rights", he pointed out the need for a bill of rights on the basis of past experience.
If it is accepted that there is a need, then the next question that arises is this. Should it be by a constitutional amendment? I pointed out at the beginning that we in parliament have certain powers under the constitution. I have referred to some of the things that took place which are unchallengeable. Should it be by statute or by constitutional amendment? If it were a constitutional amendment, that affected only the federal jurisdiction, it could be passed by both houses of parliament and would be subject to repeal at any time in the same way a statute could be repealed.
May I digress for a moment, Mr. Speaker, and say this. If a statute is passed by parliament, the experience of the past has been that subsequent parliaments are extremely loath to make any changes in a declaration that provides for freedom on behalf of the individual. In any event, if a constitutional amendment were passed affecting only the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada, it would be subject to repeal at any time by a vote of both houses as would a statute. On the other hand, I realize that there are many

who feel that there should be a constitutional amendment binding on the federal parliament and the provincial legislatures.
All I have to say in that regard is this, Mr. Speaker. Let us clear our own doorstep first. In so far as a constitutional amendment would be concerned, the experience of 80 years indicates very clearly that the provinces, jealous of their jurisdiction, would not support a constitutional amendment applicable to themselves.
A group of distinguished Canadians submitted their views on a bill of rights to the joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons in 1947. The list of those who urged members of parliament of all parties to establish a bill of rights contains the names of Canadians in every province, outstanding and distinguished in their respective fields including educators, legislators, newspapermen, representatives of labour and of industry. Indeed, it is a group of names that reads like a "Who's Who" in our country. They suggested that it should be by way of a constitutional amendment binding on the national government and the provinces.
I have answered that suggestion. We do not intend to refrain from proceeding with a bill of rights effective in the parliament of Canada or to delay that step, postpone it and ultimately not achieve action, when we have available here the power, the right and the exclusive jurisdiction to bring in a bill of rights within the constitutional power and the legislative ambit of the national government. Again I quote from Professor Lower in this regard:
The question to be initially faced is whether a bill of rights should be a simple statute or whether it should be a constitutional amendment. The latter is preferable, but at our Canadian rate of proceeding it will take many years to effect. A statute, on the other hand, is repealable. Yet such a statute would constitute a declaration of principle, it would give a text from which to preach, it would form one additional hurdle for parliament to take when it next consented to abrogation of civil liberties, and would make that abrogation a much more solemn thing than It has hitherto been.
I am not going to refer in particular to the authorities on the division of power as between the federal government and the legislatures in respect of this subject. There have been a number of them in recent years. It is interesting, Mr. Speaker, to note that there was never a case in the privy council at the time when it was our supreme law body wherein an interpretation was given of the constitutional division with respect to civil rights. Some recent cases are the Saumur case, (1953) 2 Supreme Court Reports, 299; the Winner case, (1951) Supreme Court Reports, 887 which deals with interprovincial jurisdiction; the Birks case, (1955) Supreme

Court Reports, 799; and the Switzman case, (1957) Supreme Court Reports, 285.
However, in reading these authorities one feels that the question as to the division of the constitutional power over fundamental freedoms has as yet been far from interpretation and delineation. That is another reason why we, proceeding in parliament to bring about the achievement of fundamental freedoms, must scrupulously respect whatever provincial jurisdiction exists in reference in whole or in part to this matter.
As I said a moment ago, a constitutional amendment which was passed by parliament in so far as those rights are concerned and which would permit of such a declaration being made by the federal parliament would be subject to repeal as is a statute. A constitutional amendment that went ahead and did not have regard to provincial jurisdiction whatever phase of provincial jurisdiction was concerned, would simply be declared ultra vires in so far as it infringed upon provincial jurisdiction. It is for these reasons that we have determined that the course to take is to place before parliament a statute covering those freedoms which are within the jurisdiction of parliament in so far as the laws that are passed by parliament in the days ahead are concerned, or that have been passed heretofore.
In the past there have been those who have stated that a bill or rights would make ineffective that unity of action which is necessary when our security is challenged in war. That matter has been covered by the section to which I have made reference, which gives to parliament, representing all the people, the right to take positive action when and if those freedoms must be infringed upon. Britain has had similar experience and in her tradition for freedom has followed a similar course. It is interesting to note that the bill of rights of the United States, in so far as fundamental freedoms are concerned, covers only those freedoms which are subject to legislation by congress. That is something which is often forgotten. In other words, the United States congress cannot legislate on the preservation of human freedoms except those which come within the ambit of the congress of the United States. The later provisions dealing with the civil rights of individuals and constitutional amendments may be construed as applicable to individual states, but the initial ones dealing with fundamental freedoms are entirely within the jurisdiction of legislation which can be passed by the United States congress.
I mentioned habeas corpus, and I referred to an instance when it was swept away by
Human Rights
a simple order in council. It is well to understand the position taken by Britain and by the United States in this regard. In the United Kingdom the habeas corpus act has been suspended by the British parliament. It was done in 1715, in 1745 and in 1794; it was done with respect to Ireland in 1881. This was done in each case by an act of parliament, a suspending act of a temporary nature only, and it was followed in each case by an act of indemnity to protect the executive. In the first and second world wars there was no form of suspension of habeas corpus, but wide powers were conferred on the executive by the defence of the realm act and the emergency powers act in 1914 and 1939 respectively.
In the United States the privilege of the writ of habeas corpus shall not be suspended unless when, in the case of rebellion or invasion, public safety may require it. In 1863, when it was suspended, congress authorized the president to suspend the writ and the delegated power was exercised not only by President Lincoln during that war but by President Grant during the reconstruction period.
Sir, if parliament passes this statute it will be taking a step, a major step, forward to stop the erosion of the rights of the individual within the jurisdiction of the national government. It will do more than that. I do not wish to repeat what has been said on other occasions, but I think the house will allow me to quote from my words in 1947, and, in the light of the intervening years, this still constitutes my point of view. At page 3152 of Hansard for May 16, 1947, I said:
What would a bill of rights do? It would establish the right of the individual to go into the courts of this country, thereby assuring the preservation of his freedoms.
A bill of rights would be a contract between the individuals of Canada and the government of Canada. It would assert the right of the individual: it would assert the right of a minority to be protected in the exercise of its rights, against the majority. It would, above all, assure that each of us would have a legal right to be heard in the courts of this country.
Then in 1952, as recorded at page 720 of Hansard for March 24 of that year, I said:
A bill of rights would deny the right of any majority to interfere with my serving God as my conscience demands. It would deny the right of any government to interfere with my right to speak or write so long as I did so within the law.
Later on I had this to say:
A bill of rights would redefine the landmarks of liberty, which are almost erased as a result of the pathways of war becoming the permanent highroads of peace.
When I say that, sir, it is not in criticism of any political party in this country; it is

Human Rights
a simple statement of fact. A similar situation arose in the United Kingdom because those pathways which are short-cuts in wartime are so easy to maintain that they tend to become the permanent institutions of peace.
A bill of rights would do something more; it would make parliament freedom-conscious. It would make parliament realize that rights are to be preserved. It would make parliament more cautious in passing laws that would have the effect of interfering with freedom. It would act as a landmark by means of which Canadians, through parliament, would have redeclared those things which have made Canada great. It would preserve those spiritual wells in legislative form without which freedom cannot survive. It would give to Canadians the realization that wherever a Canadian may live, whatever his race, his religion or his colour, the parliament of Canada would be jealous of his rights and would not infringe upon those rights which are dear to us all.

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
The cynics will say it does not go far enough. It is a first step. As the Chinese say, every journey by mankind, even a journey over a thousand years, begins with just one step taken by some individual who sees the possibilities for the future and tries to make it possible to equalize the opportunities for those of his own generation. This bill will not do everything, but I do think fair minded Canadians will agree that it is a major step forward.
I can only hope that Canadians as a whole will give to parliament the benefit of their suggestions and ideas in the next few months so we shall be able to make such amendments in the bill to be presented to the next parliament as will still the heart stirrings of those who fear for freedom in our country, assuring always the maintenance of the constitutional rights of provincial jurisdictions.
It will be a landmark as well for Canadians. Realize this; that henceforth, except within the limitations that security demands, Canadians will know that their rights are not to be loosely disregarded, and parliament will have before it at all times the warning which is emphasized in this bill of rights, namely that fundamental rights and freedoms within the federal jurisdiction shall not be made light of by this or future parliaments.
I shall say no more at this time. I hope we will be enabled next session to discuss this question again fully and completely, and that out of the counsel of parliament and the representations of our fellow Canadians, whatever changes should be made in this bill of rights can be made in the bill then to be

presented, always assuring that it shall be constitutionally within the powers of parliament and in no way can transgress the constitution.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will have listened with the interest which the importance of the subject demands to the words of the Prime Minister in introducing this bill. I am sure that hon. members on all sides will approve the procedure which the government has adopted with regard to it, that is, giving it first reading in the closing hours of this session and then submitting it for examination and consideration at the next session of parliament.
There can be no more important questions than those of human rights and fundamental freedoms, and no questions more appropriate for parliamentary consideration. The existence and the free exercise of human rights and freedoms are the very roots of our democratic life. When these weaken, society becomes stagnant and finally servile.
It is of course true, as the Prime Minister has said, that only preliminary consideration by three members of the house can be given to this bill at this time, and no detailed analysis seems to be called for now. But, as the Prime Minister himself has indicated, it needs very careful study indeed. I am the more impressed by the necessity of this because, to me at least, it seems a little ambiguous and unclear in places, and its effect, especially in part II, might be other than is intended. It is also unclear in my mind as to the overriding effect of this bill on other legislation which might follow and the influence it might have on such legislation. That, of course, remains to be determined.
For instance, what would be the relationship of a bill of this kind to a bill which would give the governor in council power to take citizenship away from a Canadian if upon the report of a minister the governor in council was satisfied that such a Canadian did not at the time of taking the oath of allegiance intend to comply with that oath? Yet that is in a bill which we will be discussing immediately after this one. It is therefore very difficult to come to firm conclusions as to the contribution this bill can or should make to the objective we all have in mind, the more complete and the more assured protection of human rights in this country, than which, of course, there could be nothing more important.
As the Prime Minister has said, we will all have a chance to give a more considered opinion on this matter at the next session of parliament. Today, therefore, I shall confine my remarks to the general objectives of the bill which we on this side fully and

warmly support, and to the general problem of the preservation and strengthening of fundamental rights and freedoms in our Canadian democratic society. I will try to treat this subject, and that objective, in the nonpartisan and rational manner which its nature warrants.
In discussing fundamental freedoms there is one which is not usually enrolled with the others but which, in my view, should guide our consideration, namely freedom from illusion. We have to approach this subject, if we would approach it constructively, free from illusion, though not, I hope, free from ideals. Let us ask ourselves first, then, what is the present situation in Canada with respect to our rights and our liberties, and I am talking now about the rights and liberties of the individual, without which there can be no rights and liberties of the state. What is our heritage in this matter? Are our rights and freedoms threatened and, if so, what can we do about it?
Those who talk about rights and freedoms usually refer, and quite rightly, to their parliamentary and democratic foundations in the United Kingdom as something we have inherited and something which can protect us, as something very precious which is ours both in law and in custom. And, of course, this heritage is a matter for Canadian pride and satisfaction.
The two British contributions to this heritage which seem to be an indispensable part of every speech on this subject are Magna Carta and the bill of rights of 1688. But it is interesting, as an illustration of how things can develop in a way which was never intended, to realize that Magna Carta when signed was a feudal, not a people's, declaration or charter. The rights and liberties which it embodied were those which the feudal lords demanded only for themselves against a despotic king. It had no provisions which gave rights or protection to the people, and no thought of promoting their democratic progress. The law to be observed was feudal law, and the liberties to be guaranteed were feudal franchises.
So far as the 1688 bill of rights is concerned, it did not proclaim or guarantee abstract rights or enunciate lofty democratic principles. It was a strictly practical document designed to ensure that governmental abuses of arbitrary monarchs should not recur.
In the light of history what, then, is the importance in political and democratic development of documents such as Magna Carta and the bill of rights? What meaning has this development and such documents for us in Canada? Their importance lies not in what these things meant at the time, but what
Human Rights
they were made to mean by later interpretation; in the slow progress toward popular and democratic rights, progress which would certainly have been most strenuously opposed by the barons of Runnymede and by the gentry who overthrew James II. Those documents became a symbol, and therein lies their importance for the future.
Therefore we ask ourselves, can this declaratory bill in its present form, and in our federal system, become such a symbol when the very limited authority behind it to deal with civil rights is specifically recognized in its own terms? Or-and this is another question-will this recognized limitation, enshrined in a federal statute, make progress perhaps more difficult, rather than less difficult, and hinder rather than help the effort to ensure that all Canadians, wherever they live and under whatever jurisdiction they may be, will have certain basic rights and fundamental liberties guaranteed to them, rights which cannot be diminished let alone destroyed by any legislative process from any Canadian source apart, of course, from temporary and necessary surrender during a period of war or national emergency.
That surely, Mr. Speaker, is the ideal we must seek to realize while preserving the constitutional rights of every province; while preserving also the necessity, which is a primary one but which can be abused, of ensuring the security of the state. Therefore I ask again, does this bill make any advance toward this realization? Can we do more, and how? Before we can even try to answer this question we have to consider a matter which the Prime Minister has touched on, namely the position in our country in regard to jurisdiction over these matters.
Where does the constitutional authority lie in our country to deal legislatively with civil rights and fundamental freedoms? Where lies the duty to protect and to strengthen, and the power to limit and perhaps restrict them? Does it lie in the parliament of Canada or in the legislatures of the provinces, or is it divided between them?
Well, Mr. Speaker, that is no easy question to answer with any precision, to find an answer that will cover all the circumstances. Certainly the judgments of the supreme court are not clear on the matter, though it may well be that important decisions will be made before long by that court in cases that have reached it or may in due course reach it.
The preamble to the British North America Act, which was quoted by the Prime Minister states that the provinces are united into one dominion "with a constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom". Deductions have been drawn from this and

Human Rights
impressive legal arguments advanced on it to give the federal parliament the same power over civil rights that is possessed at the present time by the parliament of the United Kingdom. Those deductions and arguments are not, I believe, confirmed by legal decisions or by constitutional practice.
After all, Mr. Speaker, the words quoted are from the preamble and not from the operative part of the British North America Act which, in terms in the operative part, gives us a constitution not unitary like that of the United Kingdom but federal, which distributes the law-making power between the central parliament and the provincial legislatures. As we know, section 92 (13) of that act gives property and civil rights to the provinces. Civil liberty and rights, therefore, it can be argued and with impressive evidence to support the argument, are in the keeping of both the federal and the provincial legislatures.
Therefore the power of parliament in this matter may mean not so much what can be done but who can do it. The courts must decide, of course, in cases of dispute which is the authority; but as I have said, our court of last resort-at least in the decisions that I have been able to study-are not very clear in this matter, at least not very clear to a layman. Parliament, incontrovertibly, does have power to make certain actions criminal offences, and this can protect civil rights. Parliament also has the broad authority under "peace, order and good government", but how far do those powers go?
The Prime Minister mentioned one or two cases. Perhaps I can mention one or two. In 1938 the Alberta press control law reached the supreme court, and three members of that court, including Chief Justice Duff, held that provincial legislatures could not limit freedom of association or of debate or of the press, and that these matters were substantially subject to federal control. But in another case the Prime Minister mentioned, the Saumur case, in 1953 five of the justices of the supreme court agreed that a province had some legislative competence in connection with freedom of religion; three, in fact, of the supreme court justices took the definite position that freedom of religion was a civil right falling within provincial jurisdiction under the civil rights provision of the British North America Act. Yet the majority of the court also refused to deny federal legislative competence in the matter, and three positively affirmed it. So where do we stand? Can our civil liberties and rights be restricted by provincial laws by giving those laws a property label? If so, where could this lead us?
On the other hand, can provincial jurisdiction be made subordinate to federal laws in this field by general application, protecting all Canadian citizens in the exercise of their fundamental rights, with punishment for those who offend against them? The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that we do not know, certainly not beyond doubt; and until we do know the question is bound to arise in our minds of the right of the parliament in Ottawa to legislate on matters which are in doubt and which are often claimed by the provinces to be within their jurisdiction. Perhaps "right" is the wrong word. Perhaps the question is more concerned with one of constitutional propriety.
The Prime Minister, as I shall attempt to show later, in the past advocated clearing up this matter by submitting a draft bill to the supreme court to determine its constitutionality, or by requesting an opinion from the court on the powers of the federal parliament in this field. This idea at the moment at least seems to have been dropped.
Another method would be a conference- and this has been referred to in debates in this house in the past-with the provinces for the purpose of seeking an agreement on this fundamental question, and afterward either to amend the British North America Act by including within it a bill of rights or to pass a bill of a less fundamental character with provincial agreement. Which of these two procedures one prefers will depend a good deal on whether one has more trust in the courts or in parliament.
There is one factor, though, that concerns constitutional amendments. If it were an amendment which covered all aspects of this question, covered all Canadian citizens in the exercise of all their fundamental rights, I believe I am right in saying that such an amendment could not be made to the British North America Act in the present circumstances except by the United Kingdom. Therefore we Canadians, in respect of a matter which concerns the rights and liberties of all Canadians, would have to go to another jurisdiction to amend our constitution to make that possible. That is something out of which no Canadian takes satisfaction.
These points, I admit, are not settled in the bill before us and it was not the intention of the bill to settle them, as the Prime Minister has pointed out. This bill is of limited scope and claims to be restricted to rights strictly within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament, whatever that jurisdiction may be.
In this respect, Mr. Speaker, this bill inevitably falls short of other proposals advanced in parliament since world war II

for the protection of the rights and liberties of Canadian citizens, including some significant ones put forward by the Prime Minister himself, one of which at least he mentioned this morning. Therefore, though it may only be a short look, I should like to look at the record of discussions on this matter that have been held in parliament. I will go back no further than 1945.
In that year a member of the C.C.F. party, the then member for Winnipeg North, made a frontal attack on the problem of the rights and liberties of the individual in Canada by proposing that a bill of rights be incorporated in our constitution as part of the British North America Act. Whether or not you agree with it, the C.C.F. took a clear-cut position on the matter then, a position which I believe they have maintained since. But that initial C.C.F. proposal was dropped in view of the fact that the government of that time was about to introduce a citizenship bill, and it was thought that there would be a discussion of this matter on that bill. But in the next year, 1946, the then member for Lake Centre, the present Prime Minister, advocated in the house a bill or declaration of rights either independently of or to be included in the citizenship bill.
In 1947 a joint committee of the house and Senate, to which the Prime Minister has referred, examined the whole matter, and there was a very interesting debate in the house on the resolution setting up that committee. The present Prime Minister had this to say in that debate, as found at page 3150 of Hansard for May 16, 1947:
Declarations regarding freedom do not assure the practice of freedom; unless the right remains for the individual or the nation to have his or its rights established under law, they are but pious declarations.
For that and for other reasons, no doubt, he argued at that time that the proposed joint committee should seek the co-operation of representatives of the provinces so that, and I quote again from page 3152, "a comprehensive bill of rights might be evolved either by way of constitutional amendment or by statute." For that purpose, as he mentioned a few moments ago, he had himself drafted a bill for the proposed committee which would have provided, to use his own words, "the assurance to Canadians" of the basic freedoms which he enunciated. He made a very powerful speech on that occasion, and I should like to quote one more paragraph from it. As found on page 3158 the present Prime Minister said:
A declaration of a bill of rights in this country would be a positive declaration on the part of men and women of all political faiths in their belief in civil liberties. Whether the federal authority has the power or not to pass legislation respecting civil
Human Rights
liberties, its passage would strengthen the hand of the Minister of Justice in the matter of the disallowance of any statute which would deny freedom anywhere in our country.
Well, Mr. Speaker, the joint committee met in 1947 and again in 1948 having, without very much success-I hope the Prime Minister will have more success between now and next session-attempted to secure opinions from the attorneys general of the provinces and the deans of the law schools on the matters before it. The provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, Manitoba and New Brunswick gave no opinion. British Columbia and Nova Scotia took the position that these matters fell mainly within provincial jurisdiction. Those deans of law schools who replied-I am not sure whether or not the Secretary of State for External Affairs was one at that time; perhaps he had advanced beyond that stage-in general expressed the opinion that the federal parliament's power was limited in this matter.
Before the joint committee the then deputy minister of justice, Mr. Varcoe, made the following interesting but very cautious statement, and I quote from his evidence to be found on page 32 of the proceedings of the committee:
You pass a declaration respecting those rights. What is that? It may be treated as a resolution of parliament, a mere declaration of the policy parliament would like everybody to adopt. It would be the equivalent, you might say, of a resolution of the two houses. I am talking of a bill of rights containing no penalty provisions and no sanctions-
That is true of this bill.
-but which is a mere declaration that individuals shall have those rights. No. 1, it may be treated merely as a resolution; No. 2, it may be said to be no statute at all because it does not produce any legal consequences. Not producing any legal consequences, you cannot tell whether it is under dominion legislation or not.
Mr. Varcoe went on to say:
When you have a division of legislative powers, you look at an act and you say, is it good or is it bad? It is good, depending upon the purpose and effect of the statute. If it has no effect and no legal purpose, then there is no way of testing whether it is good or bad.
I admit that this is a very careful approach to this problem. At that time the present Prime Minister did not approve of this cautious attitude to any great extent, and that is understandable because of his desire to get something done. In the debate in the House of Commons on April 11, 1948, the Prime Minister had this to say as found at page 2846 of Hansard:
Here we are a sovereign nation among the nations of the world and promising as a signatory of the United Nations to uphold fundamental freedoms as one of the principal prerequisites for the success of the United Nations; yet the minister's attitude-

Human Rights
He was referring to the Liberal minister of justice.
-tonight raises a doubt whether Canada even internationally can do that which all the nations of the United Nations undertook to do when the charter was accepted.

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but he has brought up something there that only he can answer. Having accepted the universal declaration of human rights in the United Nations which, I think I am right in saying, was submitted by most other democratic countries in the world to their respective legislatures, why was that declaration of human freedoms not submitted to the parliament of Canada?

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the declaration of human rights of the United Nations has been accepted by Canada.

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: No.

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Yes, I think I am right that the declaration has been accepted. If I am wrong I will be corrected. It took some years, but I think it eventually was accepted by Canada. In any event, our hesitation in respect of this declaration, and I know something about this, arose from the fact that it included matters that were strictly within provincial jurisdiction. Therefore it could not be accepted with propriety by the Canadian delegation without having all of the provinces accept at least those parts of it which entrenched on provincial jurisdiction, and that was not done by all the provinces.
The declaration, however, is one thing. The United Nations bill of rights, which is still under discussion is something else. We made it very clear at the United Nations and I have no doubt that the present government is taking the same position that the bill could not be accepted in its present form because it would be unconstitutional for us. However to get back to the debate of 1948, on the following day, April 12, the present Prime Minister also had this to say as found at page 2856 of Hansard:
Some say that the right of the provinces to abrogate and interfere with the fundamental freedoms is inherent in the British North America Act, although the preamble to that act states that our constitution shall be similar to that of the United Kingdom. Those who contend that these rights rest in the provinces aver that we in this country must be a balkanized Canada whereby an individual may enjoy certain fundamental rights in one province while in another they may be denied. It is that question of legislative jurisdiction that I am asking the government of this country to submit to the supreme court.
This was in 1948.
If it is the law, then it denies to the individual that Canadian citizenship which should be the result of the measure introduced by the Prime Minister in 1944. To say that in one part of

Canada a Canadian may enjoy freedom of religion and of speech and of association, all those great and abiding freedoms, and that in another province a Canadian may not enjoy them, is a denial of the possibility that we shall ever build a United Canada on the basis of equality of the individual before the law in all parts of the country.
During this discussion in the House of Commons the present Prime Minister proposed the two steps I have mentioned, one of which was a reference to the supreme court to find out, if possible, what powers the parliament of Canada had in this field and, second, the setting up of a standing committee of the House of Commons on civil rights, together with a civil liberties division in the Department of Justice. Neither of these steps is proposed in the bill before us.
This joint committee reported in 1948. It produced a very interesting report which I should like to read, but I do not believe I shall take the time of the house to do so. Two years later, in 1950-the Prime Minister made a reference to this-the Senate appointed its own special committee on human rights and fundamental freedoms with Senator Roebuck, who has always taken a great interest in this field, as chairman. This committee took voluminous evidence and heard many representations. It then came to the conclusion that an effective bill could only be worked out with the provinces for incorporation within the constitution, but that as an interim measure a declaration should be adopted limited to those rights within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. This was the view of the Senate committee at that time, and I take it that is the view embodied in the bill before us.
Then in the next year, 1951, Mr. Coldwell, following the consistent C.C.F. attitude on this matter, moved a resolution in this house which went further because it proposed to include in the Canadian constitution, by an amendment to the British North America Act, a declaration of human rights and liberties. The present Prime Minister, in the second session of that year when the house was discussing a bill to amend the Supreme Court Act, had this to say as recorded at page 1561 of Hansard for December 4, 1951. In again advocating the reference of a draft bill to the supreme court he said he did so to find out "what if any of the fundamental freedoms are within the jurisdiction of the federal parliament".
He brought the matter up again in 1952 with a draft bill which could be used for this purpose. Then, leaving out the intervening years when there was some discussion in the house but nothing new of significance, we find that in 1955 the present Prime Minister

again placed his draft bill before the house and requested that it should be submitted to the supreme court for an opinion on constitutionality. During that discussion, and I recall that debate, the then minister of justice, Mr. Garson, used these words:
The introduction of this deceptively simple but rather emotional issue into such a complex field creates a problem which ... is an extremely difficult one. It is the problem of superimposing a bill of rights, after the United States fashion, upon the federal constitution of Canada, whose main feature, inherited from the constitution of Great Britain, is the sovereignty of its legislative bodies-
Mr. Garson went on to say:
Now this feat . . . has never yet been accomplished in any country in the world. I might point out just one of its difficulties. It is one thing to withhold from the provincial legislative bodies legislative powers when the constitution of a country is originally formed. It is quite a different thing to withdraw from the provinces 88 years later provincial legislative powers on the strength of which at least the original provinces could argue that they entered confederation.
He said that this was involved in the issue before the house, the effect of this kind of action, whatever form it may take, upon provincial jurisdiction.
In dealing with the question of the reference to the supreme court, which used to occupy the attention of my right hon. friend, Mr. Garson said that when a question of constitutional interpretation comes before the court it usually comes in the form of a statute that has been passed. The idea Mr. Garson was expressing then was that the court should be asked to consider legislation which would deal with overt acts and not broad enunciations of desirable objectives; in other words, to consider a statute that dealt with the specific ways in which the various freedoms might be exercised or with acts which would be regarded as interference with those freedoms.
Then Mr. Garson went on to something else, and I should like to say a word about this because it seems to me to be a very important aspect of the whole question. He pointed out then what I should like to point out today, that the basic freedoms are more highly regarded and more secure to the individual in Canada than in any other country in the world, with the possible exception of Great Britain itself. We have managed to achieve that position-I am not suggesting it cannot be improved upon-without any fundamental bill of rights. Mr. Garson asked himself the question, as I ask the house, why are these rights and freedoms secure? Of course there have been infringements of them. The Prime Minister has mentioned a few from 1945 onward, and perhaps I could mention a few from 1930 to 1935.
Human Rights

speechtext: I should like to hear them.

speechtext:
In Mr. Bennett's regime there were some things done by order in council to which my hon. friend might easily take exception. However, by and large, there is no country in the world in which human rights and freedoms are more secure than in our own. Mr. Garson attempted to answer the question why in this way:
Because they are protected by the British principle of the sovereignty of parliament. It is this British principle which the hon. member for Prince Albert proposes to abridge by attaching constitutional limitations to it in the manner of the bill of rights in the United States constitution.
I am not suggesting that the position taken by the Minister of Justice at that time, in all its details, is the correct one. I am not suggesting that the position in regard to rights and liberties in this country is perfect. It certainly is not perfect in its federal or in its provincial aspects. But I am suggesting that by the method we have followed over the years we have built up in this country a respect for freedom, a respect for human rights, which is not exceeded in any other free country in the world today. So we have to look at any proposal bearing on this matter in the light of the experience we have had. We have to be very sure before we make a change that it is going to be an effective change, and a change in the right direction.
