subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Before one o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was attempting to deal with some of the legal and constitutional aspects of this question of civil rights and fundamental liberties, and to trace in a brief way the parliamentary discussions of this subject since 1945, discussions which showed how very complicated the question is, especially in a federal system, and how it is possible for one's ideas to develop and even change in the consideration of this matter.
Our basic constitutional structure in Canada that we have inherited from Great Britain is based on parliamentary sovereignty, the sovereignty of the legislatures within their own jurisdictions. A bill of rights can be passed by this house in the ordinary way, but if it is no part of our constitutional structure it can be repealed or amended any time parliament so desires. I am not underestimating the

Human Rights
importance of the argument advanced by the Prime Minister, that the very existence of a bill of this kind, dealing as it does with such important matters, may give some assurance that it will not be interfered with by subsequent legislation. But parliament remains supreme in our system and in the power given to it in our federal constitution. Under our system-and I do not think we would wish to change it-there is no absolute protection against anything that a parliament or a legislature can do within its own jurisdiction.
Have we suffered from this situation in the past? Other countries with their written constitutions and their fundamental constitutional acts can and do talk a great deal about their fundamental rights not to be touched by ordinary legislative action and, if so touched, to be protected and restored by the courts. That is the theory behind their constitutions, and the theory of parliamentary sovereignty lies behind ours.
Certainly our parliamentary system is different. If parliament defines a civil right or an individual freedom today, it becomes law and he who violates it breaks the law. That is how we have built up our edifice of fundamental freedoms and human rights. By the same token parliament can redefine and restrict a right tomorrow. But this may seem to be a theoretical weakness. Who can say that a Canadian's rights without a bill of rights are not as well established or as well protected as those of a citizen of the United States in Alabama or in Arkansas, even with his constitutional guarantees?
The measure of our rights and liberties as Canadian citizens is the enlightenment, the tolerance and the good sense of our society as it expresses itself not only in laws and in administrative practices but in social behaviour, customs and conventions. A wise, mature and confident free society will be jealous and vigilant to ensure the rights of its citizens, even if there are no written constitutional guarantees for that specific purpose. A fearful or a subdued people under an arbitrary or reactionary government will have no rights to guarantee, no matter how many resounding bills it may pass or how many eloquent declarations it may make.
Mr. Speaker, I have heard at the United Nations, advocating human rights and fundamental freedoms with eloquence and vehemence, men who were representing states whose people were ground down by dictators or in one or two cases states which actually recognize slavery in their constitutions.
No, Mr. Speaker; rights and freedoms are not established or protected merely or primarily or often at all by proclamations of

beliefs or written constitutions, but by the slow, sure building of a sound and progressive social, political and economic structure of law, justice and understanding. That has been the British way and it has worked there; and on the whole it has worked with us too.
Not only do constitutional acts or bills of rights even in free democracies not always ensure the individual of the rights and freedoms which we consider to be fundamental; arbitrary and just administration can defeat even beneficent laws and weaken the protection they are supposed to give. Furthermore, legislatures themselves and their members, even under the law, can prejudice and even destroy an individual's rights, debase his dignity and weaken his security by arbitrary investigatory processes ostensibly for the purpose of securing facts and opinions on which to base good legislation.
We have witnessed across the border legislative investigations that have degenerated into circuses or persecutions or even witch hunts. We have seen efforts made to destroy men's reputations, to violate their rights by sensational charges based on the flimsiest and most hearsay evidence, without anything approaching due process of law. There have been sordid exposures of some of the worst aspects of our democratic processes where representatives of the people have tried to fix guilt by association or assertion, by innuendo or false evidence, on those who could not defend themselves. No bill of rights in our neighbouring country was able to save some of these men. But an aroused public could and did correct many of these excesses and abuses.

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Did not the Supreme Court of the United States make some decisions?

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Yes; the supreme court did make some decisions in the United States and the courts have stepped in; but they have stepped in sometimes after the damage has been done to the rights and dignity of the person affected. Neither the court nor the constitutional law of the country was able to prevent that injustice from being done or to prevent these rights from being violated. I mention this merely to indicate that a bill of rights, unless it is constitutionally guaranteed, cannot of itself prevent these abuses, nor is there any cause for Canadians to affect smugness or superiority in this matter or to pass by on the other side with an "it can't happen here" attitude.
The debasement of our legislative process which, if and when it occurs, is one way to deprive the citizen of his rights, can happen in any free country if we are not vigilant

and alert to prevent it. A parliamentary committee can become a threat to the dignity and value of this legislative process just as a congressional committee can; and no Canadian bill of rights here, any more than the bill of rights in the United States, even though hallowed by history, tradition and experience, could of itself provide a remedy. Therefore it is not only law, but it is prejudice, injustice, fear and misunderstanding which can be the greatest menaces to democratic rights and freedoms. Against these, and the bad or merely careless people who foster and exploit them, a bill of rights cannot save us. It can help, along with a vigilant public opinion and a free and independent judiciary, but it alone cannot save us. The remedy here lies in destroying prejudice and injustice, and in eliminating fear and misunderstanding. It is not enough to express an ideal in a bill, valuable as that may be; it has to be protected in practice. The rights and freedoms of a citizen must be in his heart, to be passionately desired and in his actions, to be deserved.
A venerable and great American, Judge Learned Hand, had this to say a few years ago in one of his essays:
I often wonder whether we do not rest our hopes too much upon constitutions, upon laws and upon courts.
This gentleman is still one of the greatest luminaries of the judicial system on the other side of the line. He continued as follows:
These are false hopes; believe me, these are false hopes. Liberty lies in the hearts of men and women; when it dies there, no constitution, no law, no court can save it; no constitution, no court and no law can even do much to help it. But while it lies there it needs no constitution, no law, no court to save it.
I agree with the Prime Minister when he said this morning that the dangers to rights and freedom are always present. He quoted Professor Lower I believe twice this morning, and I wish to quote another paragraph, from Professor Lower's book The Spirit of our Institutions, as follows:
The conflict between liberty and order is never-ending and humanity oscillates between the two. Left to himself, the average man might show small concern for the common good, and anarchy would ensue. But it is equally true that, left to himself, the governor, be he civil servant, minister, or prince, would show small concern for the freedom of the average man, and despotism would ensue.
It is therefore today a wise instinct that causes us to sound the alarm that the individual's rights are in danger; it is a wise instinct that prompts us to seek ways of protecting them against the forces that would weaken them, against the growing demands and pressures of the state, and not only of the state but of the state within the state. This is a time of bigness but not always a
Human Rights
time of greatness. It is an age of consolidation of smaller units into big ones in every sphere of human activity, of concentration of power and authority. Against this bigness, this power, whether exercised by government or outside of government, the individual, the little man of the cartoonist, is having a hard time to maintain, let alone to strengthen, his rights as a free man, to keep control over his own activities, indeed to retain even a sense of his own identity-so easily can he become lost in the complicated social and economic society of our time.
This, in a free society, is partly his own fault, and it is partly our fault. He has asked and we have asked for security along with freedom. Indeed he might say to himself, our little man, of what avail is freedom if it is only freedom to fight to survive in a jungle of competitive existence? While that may be true, it is surely utterly unrealistic to ask the government to do the things for the individual which he now considers essential in the interests of his social and economic security and, at the same time, to expect the government not to grow big and powerful in the process and not to interfere more and more with our normal activities. So, Mr. Speaker, we ourselves are responsible for many of the pressures on our independence and for much of the weakening of our individual rights.
When the demand of the citizen for security is stronger than his desire for liberty and rights, then we are in danger, and no bills or declarations or constitutional guarantees will save us. So let us not deceive ourselves. This bill of itself may not be able to do very much. It is limited. I am not quarrelling with that fact at the moment, but it is limited in more ways than constitutionally-

speechtext: What does the hon. gentleman mean when he says it is limited in more ways than constitutionally?

speechtext:
I indicated this morning, Mr. Speaker, that by inclusion in the bill certain things are reserved to the federal parliament and by implication certain things are left to the provincial legislatures, and therefore by this kind of definition perhaps there may be a limitation which we do not have in mind at the present time. I am not putting this forward as a final conclusion but I do suggest, as I suggested at the beginning of my speech, that this bill will bear a great deal of examination, the kind of examination it is going to get between now and the next session, it has limitations, but this bill could do two things, and I think the Prime Minister mentioned them this morning; one, it could

Human Rights
become a target and an objective. If I may quote Professor Lower again, he had this to say:
A bill of rights at least gives us a mark to shoot at. One recognizes, of course, that no document will preserve liberty if the people are indifferent to it. Still, crutches do help a lame man to walk.
I would not like anyone to draw the inference from that statement that we are lame men in this country so far as our recognition of rights and liberty is concerned, but I am sure we all understand what Professor Lower was getting at.
Whether the present bill is in all respects adequate or satisfactory for the purpose we have in mind is something on which no doubt we will be asked to express our opinions at the proper time; but I do agree, without any qualification, that we in this house should all co-operate to make this the best bill possible, one that will be worthy of the objective we all have in mind, one that will be received with acclaim and without controversy.
When we come to the detailed consideration of the measure next session we on this side will have some positive and, I hope, some constructive suggestions which may assist to this end. Suggestions were invited by the Prime Minister this morning. Second, a bill of rights submitted in this way, examined in this way, by the publicity it gets or by the publicity which is created for it, draws attention to the importance of the subject and prepares the way for the thorough and detailed consideration which must follow.
As a prelude to that consideration I have only three suggestions to make, one of which was put forward this morning by the Prime Minister on behalf of the government; first, that there should be the widest possible circulation of the bill to organizations which have shown an interest in this question and to individuals such as deans of law schools with requests for their views and comments; second, that there should be set up next session to consider this bill a joint committee of both houses with broad powers, including the power to summon witnesses; third, and this is something even more important that might be done, that we should try to secure the support and cooperation of the provinces for any Canadian action in this field. Indeed, as a result of consultation with the provinces it might be possible to widen the action so as to include both the federal government and provincial governments in a joint declaration on individual rights and freedoms. Then indeed we would have a powerful symbol.

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: What are the hon. gentleman's hopes in that direction, on the basis of his own experience?

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: I would not like to put my hopes either very high or very low, but I have learned over the years not to give up the search for an objective because it does not seem easily attainable, I am sure the Prime Minister has learned that too.

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: If we attain the same degree of success it will be all right.

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: So I suggest to the Prime Minister that the bill be submitted to the provinces for their comments, and that before the next session of parliament he should invite the provinces to consider whether their respective legislatures should not join with the federal parliament in a truly national declaration on human rights and fundamental freedoms.

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman allow a question? I am interested in the suggestion. If that course were followed and the reaction was unfavourable would the hon. gentleman not then feel that this was the proper course?

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
It might be, depending entirely on the results of the approaches that were made. I am suggesting now that approaches should be made. I am not suggesting that if those approaches did not result in favourable action, the results should be made public. But surely if we in this country want the kind of assurance with regard to rights and liberties in which the right hon. gentleman is interested and which, in the federal sphere, he has embodied in this bill, or so he feels; if we are going to have that on a national scale to cover all jurisdictions, then at some time or other this approach has to be made. I am putting forward the possibility, at least, of making that approach in connection with all the interest which will now be raised in this matter through the introduction of this bill. Between now and the next session of parliament consideration will be given to it by private organizations and individuals. Perhaps it is not too much to expect that the provinces will also give consideration now to this fundamental question in the light of the move that is being proposed by the federal government.
In conclusion may I just say that on behalf of my party I have been honoured and privileged to speak on this subject today. Liberalism with a small "1", working as it so often has through Liberal governments with a capital "L", stands for individual rights and freedoms. Its very name implies that. It has

always recognized, however, that with every right goes a responsibility and with every freedom an obligation.
For one hundred and fifty years, and in many countries, progress toward national freedom, social justice and political democracy has been associated with the eternal principles of liberalism. Here in Canada our party can take pride in its contribution to the realization of those principles in our national life and our national development. That contribution is on the record.
We have, I admit, been cautious over the years in relying more on concrete acts than on academic declarations. We have also, of course, recognized our own special problem of federalism in Canada in respect of rights and liberties, and we have on occasion had to reconcile the demands of individual liberty and national security in ways which did not please everybody. But on the whole I believe our record in this great work of protecting and advancing the rights and freedoms of our citizens has been good. We desire to keep it so, and that spirit will govern our consideration of this matter.

subtopic: MEASURE TO RECOGNIZE AND PROTECT HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the C.C.F. party throughout the years has stood for a bill of rights guaranteeing basic human rights and fundamental freedoms. Our record on this question is clear and consistent, and as far as I know without blemish or mistake. Thus we are pleased to associate ourselves with any move that may mean progress toward that very desirable end.
Reference has been made to the many aspects of human rights and fundamental freedoms which are the subject of this bill; the right of the individual to the protection of the law without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex; freedom of religion, freedom of speech, freedom of assembly and of association, and freedom of the press. Those are the objectives or part of the objectives, of the measure; and to whatever extent this bill goes in guaranteeing those freedoms we give it our full support.
The march to freedom throughout the world is a difficult one. Along that road are many barriers and many heartbreaks, much tyranny and human suffering, but I believe that Canada together with the civilized- yes, with all the nations of the world-is moving in that direction.
If this bill of rights were as good as human ingenuity could make it; if it were as perfect as possible, the struggle for what it endeavours to guarantee would not be over. It is a continuing struggle, and if one read 57071-3-294
Human Rights
nothing else to learn of that continuing struggle than the speeches of the present Prime Minister over the years, one would know of that struggle. It is a struggle which is going on in the Canadian House of Commons very day of this session; it is a struggle that comes about because of our division- and this is what we like in our free society -into different parties and into different, groups with different responsibilities and different powers. It is the duty of the opposition in a free parliament so to conduct itself as to assure to the greatest degree it can those human rights and fundamental freedoms of which we are now thinking.
There are perhaps two schools of thought on this question. One is that those freedoms can be the better guaranteed if they are written into a bill of rights or into our constitution in concrete terms. Then there is the other school of thought toward which the Leader of the Opposition seemed to lean, that such a bill perhaps is unnecessary, or that our freedoms are best guaranteed by a free parliament and a continuing free parliament, without going to the additional work of providing such guarantees in the constitution itself.
No matter which school one accepts, parliament itself must remain free. Of course the duty of maintaining that freedom rests to a very large degree on the governor in council. As the Prime Minister said this morning I know, because of his long experience in parliament, perhaps even because of his experience in the government, there is the temptation for the executive council to take the quick road and the short cut. Therefore it is the duty of all, including the governor in council, to keep this temptation in the background.
But there is also a duty, I suggest, which falls upon the private members on the government side of the house, and because the government has such a tremendous majority in this parliament that duty becomes all the more important. That duty is not always, without question, to accept the advice of anyone within that party, whether it be a member of the cabinet, the party whip or anyone else; but when occasion arises, when feelings and convictions are strong, party considerations should be left in the background. That applies to all members, I am sure, but I think the responsibility is heavier on the government members because of this particular situation.
This morning the Prime Minister, in painting the background, in reviewing the history of acts of government in the past showing that a bill of rights is necessary, went over a great many of the times the Liberal government had interfered with individual freedom.

Human Rights
He could have included in that survey times when a Conservative government has interfered with individual freedoms.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I find the position I have to fill today a very difficult one, not only because I am speaking after the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition who have had a much greater training and longer experience in this field than I, but also because of the record of the leaders of the C.C.F. party in and out of the House of Commons in the past. It was the first leader of the C.C.F. party, Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, who himself became the victim of a government that interfered with his own fundamental rights as well as that of others. I refer to the experience of the Winnipeg strike in 1919, and the immediate passage at that time of amendments to the Criminal Code and the Immigration Act. The amendment to the Criminal Code, which later became known as section 98, remained until 1936. The amendment to the Immigration Act gave the government the power to deport a foreign-born citizen without recourse to the courts and a fair trial. These were two instances of a government which interfered with human rights and fundamental freedoms.
One could mention the interference by the R.C.M.P. in a peaceful meeting at Regina in 1935, which subsequently became known as the Regina riot. I was quite a young boy at that time. I was a country boy who felt it was a great event to be allowed to come to the city once or twice a year. I saw those unemployed men walking the streets looking for food, looking for jobs, with a sign on their backs, "On To Ottawa". When they gathered on the market square the R.C.M.P. were turned on them and a riot took place.
One could mention, as has already been mentioned, the Alberta press act, which endeavoured with little success, because of a reference to the supreme court, to interfere with the freedom of the press. One could also mention the interference that has taken place in recent years as far as the rights of members of Jehovah's witnesses are concerned. One could also mention the padlock law.
The Leader of the Opposition has said that Canada's record may be good. Undoubtedly it is good. Maybe it is second only to the record of the United Kingdom, but it is a record in which there is a good deal that none of us is proud of today. I know that all of us would seek to remove any discrimination against persons because of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex. I know it has grieved us all recently and at other times to learn of the discrimination
IMr. Argue.]
that has taken place in the great country to the south, discrimination in regard to the rights of citizens of that country because of their colour.
I was surprised and disturbed to see reports of race riots in the city of London, England. We know that Canada's record is not completely good in this regard, that there has been discrimination in this country because of colour. We saw on television a few nights ago coloured persons who came to Canada from the West Indies, who said they experienced certain discrimination in looking for places to live and in seeking employment in our country. In recent years, as the Prime Minister has said, Japanese Canadians have been deprived of their property, have been dispersed across this country and their rights have been interfered with.
There are many people who could make a contribution in the place I am today much better than I can. One person, the late J. S. Woodsworth, I have already mentioned. Another person is Angus Maclnnis, who sat in this house as member for the constituency of Vancouver East from 1930 to 1953, and from 1953 to 1957 as the member for Van-couver-Kingsway.
I do not know of anyone I have met who was more fearless or more consistent in his fight for human rights and fundamental freedoms. His was a voice in parliament against what was being done to the Japanese Canadians in the late years of the war and immediately after, a voice without fear even though many people in the province of British Columbia told him that it was a foolish and ridiculous stand for him to take from the point of view of his own political welfare. But without fear, yes, without concern for himself in a political sense, he fought against that discrimination, and I understand that he was recently honoured by the University of British Columbia conferring on him a doctorate of laws degree arising out of his great service to the Canadian nation, including his service in fighting for the fundamental rights and freedoms of all Canadians no matter the colour of their skin.
The Leader of the Opposition has said very fairly that a resolution was moved in the house in 1945 by the member at that time for the constituency of Winnipeg North, Mr. Alistair Stewart. The Prime Minister is on the records of the House of Commons in earlier years as advocating the same objective, but as far as I have been able to ascertain Mr. Stewart was the first member of parliament to present a resolution to the house on the question. This resolution, as set

forth in Hansard for the second session of 1945 at page 900, reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, there should be incorporated in the constitution a bill of rights protecting minority rights, civil and religious liberties, freedom of speech and freedom of assembly; establishing equal treatment before the law of all citizens, irrespective of race, nationality or religious or political beliefs; and providing the necessary democratic powers to eliminate racial discrimination in all its forms.
This motion was dropped on the assurance of the then secretary of state, now the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), that some of the things Mr. Stewart had presented in his motion would be discussed and dealt with in a citizenship bill that was to follow. Similar motions were moved in the house by Mr. Stewart on many occasions. I think he set forth most vividly in a few words the meaning and purpose of a bill of rights. These words are contained in a speech he delivered in the house on May 16, 1947. As found at page 3161 of Hansard he said:
We realize that there are two paths ahead, either one of which we as free agents may choose to follow as we will. One path leads to heights of splendour yet undreamed of; the other to the darkness of hatred and strife. One leads to a realm where the human spirit will rise triumphant over the bigotries and persecutions of our age, where racial discrimination and intolerance of another's religious beliefs will be regarded as crimes against all mankind; where freedom of speech will be the inalienable right of every citizen; where men will no longer exploit their fellowmen for private gain; where every man will be the master of his soul. That is one path we can choose. The other path can lead only to that spiritual desolation to which our enemies would have consigned us.
I trust and believe that parliament and the people of Canada are choosing the first path. There has been a good deal of discussion of this question in the house and in the committee of the Senate, and certain suggestions have been made as to what course might be followed. In addition to the suggestions that have come from the Senate, one province of Canada has a comprehensive bill of rights- I refer to my own province of Saskatchewan -which is enacted to protect certain civil rights and which was assented to on April 1, 1947. The Saskatchewan bill of rights is comprehensive and is supported by all the people of Saskatchewan no matter what their political persuasion. It deals with these fundamental rights; the right to freedom of conscience, the right to free expression, the right to free association, the right to freedom from arbitrary imprisonment, the right to elections, the right to employment, the right to engage in occupations, the right to own and occupy property, the right of access to public places, the right to membership in professional and trade associations, the right 57071-3-294J
Human Rights
to education-a rather complete act, and one which I think has served a very useful purpose.
I have said that the Senate inquired into the possibility and advisability of a bill of rights. In their report in 1950 they had this to say about a basic conception:
As a result of its inquiries, your committee is assured that there are a very large number of persons in Canada who are deeply interested in the subject of human rights and fundamental freedoms and that much thought has been devoted by our citizens to the subject. That every man, woman and child has rights is generally accepted as axiomatic and that such rights should be protected is a conviction as universally held.
Your committee also agrees with this view, holding that every human being irrespective of mere classifications on account of race, creed, sex, caste or colour, and other like distinctions has rights which flow from his divine creation. The brotherhood of man results from the fatherhood of God, and a fundamental equality among men necessarily follows. Such rights are not created by men, be they ever so numerous, for the benefit of other men, nor are they the gift of governments. They are above the power of men to create. They may be violated by men, but not with impunity. They should be recognized and every care should be taken to preserve them inviolate.
Professor Frank Scott, an eminent authority, appeared before the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on human rights on April 25, 1950. Professor Scott is head of the law faculty of McGill University. He is a recognized authority on the question, and we in the C.C.F. are proud of the fact that for many years he was national chairman of our movement. He is perfectly bilingual, and I know he has always in mind in all aspects the rights of the people of the province of Quebec as well as the rights of all other Canadians. He had this to say in part in his submission to that committee:
Despite these advantages in a federal bill of rights, I do not personally consider that it would be as valuable a protection for human rights and fundamental freedoms as a bill of rights written into the constitution itself by an amendment to the B.N.A. Act. This is where a bill of rights belongs, in the fundamental law of the land.
The superior advantages of this method of protection seem obvious. There is first of all no problem of dominion-provincial jurisdiction to consider; it is just as easy to enumerate rights under provincial as rights under federal authority, since ultimately the constitution must be amended to give the bill the force of law. All that need be decided is which rights we wish to safeguard. In selecting these, we have the great advantage of the international declaration of human rights to guide us, as well as the very helpful draft which was included in the terms of reference of this committee, and others that are available.
The committee seemed to be impressed with the submission by Professor Scott, in their report they suggest that the course he outlined should be followed. For a number of years in this house Mr. M. J. Coldwell moved a motion asking for a bill of rights in a

Human Rights
certain form. I had the honour of placing this resolution on the order paper during this session as a private member's resolution. It was not possible, nor was it desirable, to have the motion moved in the light of the government's own legislation or proposed legislation in this regard.
This resolution, I believe, will be of interest to members of this house as well as to people who make a great study of this whole question. The resolution in part is as follows:
That in the opinion of this house, consideration should be given to the advisability of taking whatever steps are necessary to amend the British North America Act so as to include therein the following heading and sections:
XII Human Rights
148. Notwithstanding anything in this act, it shall not be lawful for the parliament of Canada or the legislatures of any of the provinces to make laws:
(a)	Abridging freedom of speech and expression, or freedom of religion, or of the press or other means of communication or the right of lawful assembly, association or organization.
(b)	Depriving any person of life or liberty by arbitrary or abusive measures, or denying to any person the equal protection of the laws.
(c)	Requiring or imposing excessive bail or cruel or unusual punishment or exiling Canadian citizens.
(d)	Subjecting any person to unreasonable interference with his or her privacy, family home or correspondence.
(e)	Subjecting any person to arbitrary arrest or detention or denying to any person the right after arrest to be informed promptly of the charges against such person and to trial within a reasonable time or to be released.
(f)	Suspending the right of habeas corpus or depriving any person of a fair trial or the right to be represented by counsel.
We have looked over this bill, and we can say that it is not as comprehensive as we had expected and is not drafted in the form we had desired. The C.C.F. stand over the years has been consistent. It is that the British North America Act itself should be amended. We believe that if that were done it would provide a stronger guarantee, a more certain guarantee, than a bill of rights which becomes part of our statute law.
We also feel that there is a very serious omission in this bill, in that there is no right to employment, there is no guarantee that in employing persons there will not be discrimination.

unwillingness and probably an inability to come to grips with the basic problem that exists with respect to our imports and our exports.
In 1932 and 1933 when the C.C.F. was formed expression was given to this question of the controversy between the free traders and the protectionists. The general thought expressed was that that controversy was fast becoming obsolete. Twenty-five years later we still say that it is obsolete, and even more obsolete than it was when our organization was formed. We made suggestions in 1933. We suggested the establishment of import-export boards in order to enable us to make the best possible trading agreements with other countries. Naturally we, as are other countries, are obliged to rely on trade, either importing from or exporting to other countries. By the establishment of such import-export boards, by the study and the planning of requirements, we would be able to stop the exploitation of our primary producers and, in the final analysis, stop the exploitation of the consumers of Canada in this particular case.

We submit that the bill itself or the extension of the things contained in the act at the moment which are objectionable will not help a great deal. They merely have the effect of aggravating and prolonging what is an antiquated system of dealing with our trade relationships with other countries in importing and exporting.
Over the years the C.C.F. has freely offered its proposals and its programs to governments in office and governments in the past have freely availed themselves of the things which we have proposed. We believe that in the field of international trade there needs to be economic planning; we believe that the system of tariffs as such is fallen into disuse as an adequate instrument in our economy to maintain full employment; we believe that planning of our production at home and planning of our imports by contracts between nations concerned with trade, by quotas and even exclusive quotas under certain conditions and for certain periods, are much more scientific and are in the real interests of employees in textiles and other industries and therefore are much more in the interests of the working people of Canada than is the present bill under consideration.

What we are protesting in respect of this legislation is not anti-dumping but the arbitrary features of this legislation;-firstly the violation of the right of parliament and not the minister or the government to tax and, secondly, the violation of GATT and of our other international trade obligations and of the desirable policy of expanding trade by reducing trade barriers which over the years has always given us prosperity when followed and when departed from has always at least coincided with the disappearance of prosperity. It is for those reasons that no matter how eminent or how influential the supporters of this legislation outside the house may be, it seems to me that we have

a duty inside this house to exercise our own judgment, uninfluenced by pressures from outside, as to what is best for the country as a whole.
There can be no question that no advantage will accrue to any industry from these changes in legislation unless it has the effect of keeping out goods from other countries. That is its purpose, that is its design. If that were not its design it would not be before us at all. In a country which depends for the income of one-third of its people on selling goods abroad-and I say that, representing as I do a province which depends for, I suppose, about 80 to 90 per cent of its income on selling its products outside of Canada-it is impossible for me to conceive that Canada, at a time when the United States has been giving an example of maintaining the policy of reciprocal trade agreements about which we were very worried, and at any rate holding the line in the right direction, that this country which has so much bigger stakes in foreign trade than has the United States should be moving in the opposite direction.

This is a difficult bill on which to speak on second reading, as the Leader of the Opposition discovered, because it does refer to various clauses to which one has to refer in order to deal with the bill as a whole, and without violating the rule of the house and speaking as if we were in committee, we still have to refer to the clauses

as the Leader of the Opposition did. I will follow that precedent because otherwise it is impossible to deal with this subject adequately.
It has been an interesting debate and rather a surprising one. I have heard so many things said about the Customs Act and about customs duties which bear no relation to fact whatsoever that I began to wonder whether we were debating the Customs Act or whether we were debating something in a field entirely foreign to that measure.
The Leader of the Opposition, of course, took a very pessimistic view of this bill. He foresaw the death of responsible government, the transference of power from parliament to the executive and, what is even worse, he saw power being exercised by a bureaucracy. Altogether this bill was going to have fatal consequences. The hon. gentleman also referred to section 38, to which the Prime Minister referred a few moments ago and he suggested that section 38 was, perhaps, wrong; that perhaps the Liberal party had been in error in leaving it on the statute books all these years. However, he told the house even if they did leave it on the statute books they never used it once after they came into power in 1935 until June, 1957. That, Mr. Speaker, raises an interesting question in political morality-whether it was right to have introduced it if the hon. gentleman can boast that he never used it until his party was on the way out. But that is something which the Leader of the Opposition can deal with.
Actually it was a speech full of forebodings. It reminded me of his speech on the C.B.C. prophesying doom and extinction. Now we have talk about the doom of the Canadian export industry and about the doom and extinction of the Canadian parliament as well. It seems as though the hon. gentleman is suffering from a psychosis of some kind. I suppose that if he were to visit a psychiatrist about it his trouble would be diagnosed as acute depression and melancholia following two shocks received one on June 10, 1957 and one on March 31 of this year. I suggest that the hon. gentleman and some of his friends should go to a psychiatrist. We hope this session will conclude in a few hours, perhaps, and I hope that as a result of the rest and leisure which will be available to them in the next few months they may recover some mental equilibrium and come back in January or February with a more optimistic outlook on life.

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition says that the fundamental principles of valuation have gone in this bill and for those old principles there is to be substituted executive action, bureaucratic administrative control. I want to say as positively as I can, Mr. Speaker, that the Leader of the Opposition is just as wrong in that analysis as he was in the statement with respect to the use of section 38 between 1935 and 1953. No one knows better than the Leader of the Opposition and myself how technical this matter is. You cannot deal with it in the house in such a way, I think, as to make it too obvious or too apparent just what arguments there may be. I am the first to admit that the subject is so technical that I cannot always appreciate it, and I have to be governed by information and advice which I get-and which I get naturally-from officials of whom this house well knows.
But the fundamental principle, as the Leader of the Opposition will admit, has always been the fair market value in the country of origin. This has been the principle under which tariff administration has been carried on in this country with such departures as may have been brought about under Bennett or Mackenzie King, or whoever it may be. This has been the fundamental principle. I think we can agree on that.
How is that fundamental principle established? There are two subprinciples to start with. In the first place, is it like goods; is it goods which are like the goods sold in the country of origin? If so, that value applies to them. That principle is maintained in this bill, Mr. Speaker. That principle is set forth in section 36 of this bill. It is true that there is a slight change in wording; it is true that there have been some administrative practices which have been going on throughout the years which have been codified and put into subsections, of section 36. Generally speaking, section 36 deals entirely and only with values of like goods. I say, Mr. Speaker, there has been no departure from the preceding practice or the existing law whatever in so far as section 36 is concerned.

We come to section 37. What is the situation there? We get similar goods, and that creates a much more difficult problem. Like goods, by custom practice and by custom law, means exactly like goods. There is no deviation whatsoever-there are some very minor ones such as difference in colour, perhaps, in textiles or something of that kind-but we have the words "like goods" accepted. They have to be like goods. The word "like" is spelled with a capital "L" to use a slang expression.
Then we come to similar goods, and the preceding government of which the hon. member was a member at one time shifted from similar goods to equivalent goods. Then, in 1955, they came back to the expression "similar goods". There again you run into great difficulties in interpretation. The words "similar goods" are not spelled with capitals all the way through. It means very similar, and you cannot follow that principle too far. Let me give one simple illustration. Fluid containers may have a different size in the United States from what they have in Canada. You may get a 12 ounce container in one country and a 10 ounce in the other. Are these similar or not? The product is similar; the container is similar whether it carries carrots or lima beans, but the size of the container is different. For customs administration you can say, what are two ounces? The importer may be getting a break, or he may be paying more because he is paying on the value of similar goods in the United States. Can you carry that to 15 ounces; can you carry it to 20 ounces? Of course, you cannot. You can only follow that "similar goods" principle in a very narrow line up or down when it comes to size. I use that simple illustration, but there are scores of others which could be used. Therefore, you cannot carry the "similar goods" practices too far and in the end you are driven to something else. The preceding government was driven to the use of subsection 6 of section 35 of the old act.
That was used by the preceding government and is being used today. When you look at subsection 6 of section 35 what do you find?
When the value for duty cannot be determined under the preceding subsections for the reason that
(a)	like or similar goods are not sold for use or consumption in the country of export, or
(b)	there is no established market in the country of export for like or similar goods,
the value for duty of the goods shall be such value as the minister determines.
That is, if you like, administration by bureaucracy but that has been the administration which has gone on and is going on under Nowlan at the moment, which went on under McCann, which went on under Ilsley and which has gone on under every minister of 57071-3-2951
Customs Act
national revenue since there has been a Department of National Revenue. Apparently hon. gentlemen opposite did not realize perhaps any more than I did, certainly any more than I did a few months ago, how the Customs Act has to be administered and the departmental practices which have to be worked out and which have been worked out and that instead of trying to make them more rigid and more embracing in this bill we are trying to codify them in accordance with the law that has been laid down by the courts. We have adopted the formulas and have made them more flexible than the practices are up to this minute because this bill has not yet been passed.

We come now to section 39 which is the one new section in the bill, and it is one which undoubtedly involves a change of principle from what has been done during the last few years. We heard a great deal the other day about the Bennett buggy and the shades of Bennett were dragged forth from the tomb. It was suggested that perhaps those of us on this side of the house were a reincarnation of Bennett in attempting to bring this section back into being. We have been told about the evils and the wrongs which are done in trying to impose a valuation including cost plus. What does the section do? All it says is that in computing the value for duty you shall take the cost of production, which is clearly defined in the act as being the actual cost, plus a reasonable mark-up for gross profit, and the formula for arriving at gross profit is set forth in the bill before us. Therefore everything is done according to the code, according to the rules, instead of being done haphazardly as heretofore.
But this was not Bennett. We have heard a great deal about the purity of the Liberal government and with that I will not quarrel at the moment because this reinforces the argument. The same provision as found in section 39 of the bill was in the Customs Act of Canada when Mr. Mackenzie King came into power in 1935 and he kept it there until 1948 when GATT was introduced. This is not Bennett; this is Chevrier. This is not our friend from Bonavista-Twillingate. He was in the closet writing the speeches but he was not actually in the cabinet himself. The Leader of the Opposition was not even in the closet but he was not far removed. They talk about Bennett but the section which was taken out of the act in 1948 was more rigorous, more inflexible and more onerous. The Leader of the Opposition smiles.

Its effects will be beneficial on the general economy of this country if it is administered in accordance with the general principles laid down in this bill. Let us please not go back into history. And 39. There is one other matter on which I want to spend a little more time because it may be somewhat difficult to refer to it again. I refer to the relation between this bill and the general agreement on tariffs and trade. The minister said the other day, and repeated it this afternoon that, in accordance, no doubt, with advice he has received, that this bill does not violate any of the provisions of GATT. This is a very important matter because if it does in fact violate that agreement we are ourselves subject to retaliation should this bill become law; also we shall certainly be in a much weaker position when we attempt to invoke the clauses of GATT against other countries with regard to practices which they may see fit to introduce against our exports.
There are two articles of GATT which are especially relevant to the questions raised by this bill. Article V describes the general method which should be used in determining the value for duty, and article 19, which is the so-called escape clause, entitles a country to suspend its obligations under the agreement under certain circumstances. As to article 7, I want to put this on the record because we on this side think we should relate some of the clauses in this bill to this particular article of the agreement. Article 7 in subsection 2(a) reads as follows:
The value for customs purposes of Imported merchandise should be based on the actual value of the imported merchandise on which duty is assessed, or of like merchandise, and should not be based on the value of merchandise of national origin or on arbitrary or fictitious values.
Then, subsection (c) which follows goes on:
When the actual value is not ascertainable in accordance with subparagraph (b) of this paragraph, the value for customs purposes should be based on the nearest ascertainable equivalent of such value.
That means in simple language that you have to use fair market value if you possibly can, and if you cannot use it you are given other alternatives which can be applied, but only and after an effort has been made to find fair market value. Those are the general principles. It is true that article 6 does contain an anti-dumping provision which states very specifically that safeguards against dumping are allowed under certain conditions, but only in the form of a special duty as described in section 1, not in the form of a special system of valuation. Section 7 of article 6 has this to say:

No measures other than anti-dumping or countervailing duties shall be applied by any contracting party in respect of any product of the territory of any other contracting party for the purpose of offsetting dumping or subsidization.
Then there is the escape clause which I have mentioned, and I want to put that on the record because we will be referring to it later. It is defined in part in paragraph 1A of article 19 as follows:
If, as a result of unforeseen developments and of the effect of the obligations incurred by a contracting party under this agreement, including tariff concessions, any product is being imported into the territory of that contracting party in such increased quantities and under such conditions-
I emphasize these words, because they are not the words of the bill-
-as to cause or threaten serious injury to domestic producers-
The word there is "threaten".
-in that territory of like or directly competitive products, the contracting party shall be free, in respect of such product, and to the extent and for such time as may be necessary to prevent or remedy such injury, to suspend the obligation in whole or in part or to withdraw or modify the concession.
That is a clause which has been used by certain governments as an escape from their obligations under GATT when the conditions are applicable and we have taken in Geneva, and I am sure the minister takes the same view now, a very watchful position with regard to the application of this clause. We have done our best to prevent governments, and especially the United States, invoking this clause in a way which would do damage to our exports and to our agricultural exports especially.
A country cannot use this clause unless goods are imported under such conditions as to cause or threaten serious injury to domestic producers and when it does use the clause it exposes itself to retaliation as indicated in subsection 3(a). I do not wish to put this clause on the record now because I do not want to take up much more time, but with these clauses of GATT in mind I want to look at the bill to see to what extent its clauses violate these provisions in the agreement or to what extent they are not in harmony with the objective and spirit of the general agreement.
The minister has said there is no such violation. We on this side contend that there is a violation, and that is a very important difference between us.
Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I could call it five o'clock.

The house resumed, from Friday, August 29, consideration in committee of Bill No. SD-199, for the relief of William Harrison Terry-Mr. McCleave-Mr. Rea in the chair.
On section 1-Marriage dissolved.

Mr. Chairman, the last time this committee dealt with this bill I just had the opportunity to get to my feet. At that time I was dealing with the very dangerous precedent that was set by the action taken on this particular bill. I reviewed briefly the history of the bill. Most of us are familiar with the fact that it was passed by the committee of the other house. It was turned down by the committee of this house. It was recommitted, reheard and now it is back before us again.
The reason I believe it is setting a rather dangerous precedent, Mr. Chairman, is that if this is carried through to its logical conclusion we would find that a case of this kind could come up, be presented and if it was successful, fine. If it were not successful, then the sponsors could say, "We will produce another witness and have another go

Private Bill-Divorce
at it, and if that is not sufficient then we will produce another witness and go through it all again". This could go on ad nauseam and make it even a greater farce than it is and have, as one member expressed it, divorce by automation. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in the future I think we should exercise more care along this line.
Let me deal with the case itself. From the evidence given at various hearings that it has had we are told that there were two reasons why the petitioner in this case first became suspicious of the circumstances. The first was he had noticed that his children were referring to the co-respondent as Uncle Al. The second reason he gave was neglect of the children and the fact that he was not satisfied with the way in which the children were being raised. He said these were the factors which caused him to have certain suspicions and to engage the services of certain private detectives to investigate and compile grounds for divorce.
Now, with regard to the two reasons he gave, it was also established through evidence given that the co-respondent in this case had been a friend of the family for a period of some 15 years, I believe long before the husband and wife separated in the first instance. Furthermore, there was no hint of any kind that the co-respondent in this case had been a factor when the husband and wife separated originally, because at that time although things had come to such a pass that the husband and wife felt compelled to separate and take up separate homes there was no suspicion in any way, shape or form that the co-respondent and the woman were carrying on illicit relations.
In addition to this, the oldest child appeared before the committee. I do not know whether he made the same impression on other .members of the committee as he did on me, but he certainly did not appear to me to be a child who had been neglected at any time.
In regard to his training,-and that specifically was one of the matters that the petitioner mentioned-he took exception to the table manners that the youngster was developing. I assume it was not only table manners but manners in general because I think you will find that as a rule with children growing up their table manners are no better or no worse than any of their other manners.
I certainly feel that the boy made a very good impression on the committee and his evidence raised considerable doubt in my mind as to the validity of the reasons given when this investigation was first started. I would also say that it would be quite a normal thing for a child to refer to a friend

of the family as uncle Alec when the boy, who is now 19, had known him since he was four years old. I do not think one should take anything improper out of that fact.
According to the evidence, these detectives were engaged on January 11 and over a period of six to seven months they kept a constant watch on the respondent and co-respondent. But I think one of the most significant things about the whole case was that while they claimed to have watched these two people over this long period they apparently had no idea they were being watched and thus would be acting perfectly normally. They would not have their guard up if they were implicated in anything wrong.
In spite of this fact not one bit of evidence was given by any of the five so-called detectives to indicate any sign of affection between these two people during all this long period. Where you have people who are supposed to be indulging in what these people were alleged to have been doing, I ask the committee if it is normal that there should be no sign of affection? They were never known to place their arms around each other, never known to embrace or to kiss each other during that time.
In a case of this kind where you have some witnesses testifying one way and others testifying completely the opposite and are not able to rely on completely contradictory evidence, you then have to look at other factors. I think one very important point in this case is a comparison of the witnesses. We must remember that on the one side there were five full-time or part-time detectives, five people who are commonly re-fered to as professional witnesses. They were there for one express purpose, to testify to certain things. On the other hand, you have the testimony of people who were not professional witnesses. Furthermore, they are under the added disadvantage that they do not have the benefit of notes as to times, dates and places that are available to the professional witnesses.
I am sure that if any hon. member of this committee was asked where he was on the night of July 9 last year he would be very fortunate indeed if he could remember. It would be something extraordinary if you could remember even where you were at that time, let alone any of the particulars. I am sure that a good lawyer could make you look pretty silly on cross-examination if you tried to remember too many details.
As I say, the five detectives all had notes and referred to them on various occasions. In spite of that, however, there were many instances where they gave contradictory evidence. Some of them have been mentioned

already. First of all, there was contradictory evidence as to footsteps on the stairs. One heard this, another heard that and another heard something else. There was contradictory evidence as to the covering on the stairs. Some thought they were covered with a carpet, some thought they were not, some thought they were covered with linoleum, and apparently they were not too sure what was on the stairs.
This was a very important factor, particularly in relation to the evidence given in respect to the sound of footsteps on the stairs. There would be a considerable difference in the noise caused by the footsteps of people going up or down the stairs depending upon whether they were covered with a carpet or were bare. The same thing was true of the hallway. Some of them thought there was a carpet and others thought not. In fact, I think the chairman of the committee mentioned that the witnesses even disagreed as to the layout of the hallway itself and where the stairs were going down into the basement.
There was contradictory evidence whether the lights were on or off. I suggest to the committee that they should consider which parties should know whether the lights were on or off, these professional people who go there for an express purpose or other people who may be surprised by the entry of a group of men. There was contradictory evidence as to the lights both inside and outside. One witness said that the house was in total darkness and was in a very dark location on the street and that as a result they would have been able to tell if there were any lights on in the house. Another of the professional witnesses stated that there was a street light right in front of the door. Surely these are matters on which there should be no conflict whatsoever.
Another very vital point on which there was conflicting evidence had to do with the doorbell. Some of the witnesses stated that they rang twice, that they rang the doorbell once for a period of about a minute and then rang it for a shorter period. We found that it was not a ring at all because the doorbell was of the chiming type and chimed twice for the front door and once for the back door.
There was conflicting evidence as to the clothes worn by the various parties. There was conflicting evidence as to what happened when this couple was being followed by two detectives. One stated that they used two cars and the other stated that each had his own car. There was also other conflicting evidence. The detectives were supposed to have watched these premises on previous occasions. They claimed that in some cases they had watched the house all night long but we find that on one occasion they were chased away from the
Private Bill-Divorce
area by the police. If they were chased away once, why were they not chased away on other occasions? Under the circumstances it is stretching the credibility of hon. members to ask them to believe in whole or even in part the evidence submitted by these various witnesses.
We had evidence given before the committee to the effect that the back door was not watched on all occasions. One of the witnesses went further and admitted that it was quite possible for a person or persons to go out the back door and cross the backyard to this hotel where the cars were parked without even being seen from the front. It appears that the only time the back door was watched was on the night of August 30, and strangest of all is the fact that as soon as some activity was observed in the house the ones who were delegated to watch the back door immediately left their post and raced around to the front door. It was submitted in evidence also, and I do not think it was refuted in any way, that apparently while they tried to break the front door in the back door was unlocked all the time. This evidence proves that any number of people could have left by the back door while they were trying to break in the front door. All in all, in my opinion, the evidence submitted by these five professional witnesses certainly left a great deal to be desired.
On the other hand, we have the evidence given by the respondent and co-respondent. I think all hon. members can agree that they were either telling the truth or they were the two best liars that have ever appeared before a committee. I do not believe that there is any other conclusion we can draw from the evidence given by these two witnesses. It is possible that they are not telling the truth, but again I say that is stretching the imagination a little bit. They both gave their testimony and stood up to a very rigorous cross-examination. In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, they both acquitted themselves very well. Mention was made of the fact that the co-respondent, on one or two minor matters, was crossed up, particularly in regard to the day in question and the fact of whether he did or did not have lunch. But, Mr. Chairman, I am sure all hon. members realize that that "cross-up", if you want to call it that, occurred at the end of two hours and twenty minutes of cross-examination, without a single break, by a very capable lawyer and by a group of capable lawyers who were members of the committee. Anyone who has had experience with cross-examination knows that if you have a prefabricated story you are going to get crossed up on more than one little point in a period of over two hours.

Private Bill-Divorce
In a case like this, when you have evidence that is as contradictory as that given, you are faced with a situation where you have to believe one thing or the other. You cannot believe part of one story and part of the other. It comes down to a straight matter of credulity. Who are you going to believe?
I would suggest what happened in this case, if I may, Mr. Chairman. These detectives were hired away back in January. I do not know the cost of the detectives in a case of this kind, but I can assume it is fairly high. I submit that what could have happened, and what possibly did happen, was that the detectives bled the petitioner dry by keeping this case going and going. I believe that finally the petitioner laid down an ultimatum, either you get the goods or you get off the payroll and I will get somebody else. This is the reason we have these doors being smashed down and the attempt to make a case out of the fact that one party was found upstairs and the other party in the basement. I suggest that if detectives, three or five or whatever number was working on this case, cannot come up with a better case than this then they either have not done a very good job or there was not very much upon which to work in the first place.
I submit that the explanation given by the respondent and co-respondent is the logical explanation. These are things that could well have happened. I am sure that over a period of seven or eight months many hon. members were in far more compromising positions than the one in which these two people were found on that day, yet this does not mean they were guilty of anything. Once again I say that the stories given by the two witnesses for the defence are logical. These things could have happened, and I believe they did happen. I say, Mr. Chairman, that this bill should be thrown out.

Earlier this afternoon, I was put on the spot in connection with a bill on which every party in this house agreed. We set it aside at that time. It is a principle of law, in at least eight of the provinces of Canada, that a person can come into court, ask for relief and get justice or get hurled out. At least they know where they stand. It so happens that in two provinces the people are so unfortunate that they have to come to parliament for a divorce and have their affairs dragged through the House of Commons. This should be a forum for the highest form of debate, not the lowest. We have gone into all these matters in the committee, and the committee has made a decision. I think that in fairness to the people concerned we should accept that decision or we should throw out the bill. We should submit the matter to a vote this afternoon.

I should like to say a few words on this case. Like the chairman of the committee, I think it is unfortunate that these cases have to come to parliament. Some of them are very close to the borderline, and this is one bill for which I cannot vote. I do not believe there is sufficient evidence to prove adultery. I have had considerable experience in listening to evidence, and when the evidence points as consistently to innocence as it does to guilt in any set of circumstances, then the petitioner would never succeed in a court of law. I know it is true that in parliament we are not bound by the ordinary rules of procedure that govern courts. We are not bound to refuse to grant a divorce if adultery is not proven because we can grant a divorce upon any ground. Personally, I am not satisfied that there was any ground proven upon which a divorce should be granted. I have read the evidence carefully. Many of the other members heard the witnesses the second time, although I did not have that privilege. As a result of shrewd inquiries made, I do not think there is much change. The second evidence was not recorded. In view of that situation, I certainly could not vote to support the case. I certainly shall be obliged to vote against it and I felt that I should put myself on record before doing so.
I do not believe that this parliament should be made a place in which to grant a divorce for something which has not been proved. If there are other grounds upon which this marriage should be dissolved, then the parties should come forward and substantiate the claim on those grounds. But I sincerely believe that there are no grounds of adultery on which to grant this divorce. Nothing was proved. The circumstances in which the detectives found these people point to innocence as well as to guilt, but more towards innocence. These people were good people. Why should we break up two families? That is something that could happen as a result of our granting a divorce. By doing so it would mean that we have refused to believe the evidence of the respondent and the person involved. I think it is only fair to give the benefit of the doubt to those who deserve it. I shall therefore be obliged to vote against this bill.

As the committee will know, this matter was first resolved by the committee with the dismissal of the petition. There was a recommittal and some further evidence was heard, particularly the evidence of the co-respondent. The hon. member who has just taken his seat undertook to express his views on the matter from his experience. May I say, Mr. Chairman, that I happen to be a lawyer with 31 years of experience. In

my experience I have never before heard such an unmitigated liar as was that corespondent when he came before the committee. This case has been proved to a point where, I submit, any court of law would decree a divorce. As the hon. member for Halifax stated, it is a travesty of justice if people are to be put in a different position when they come to parliament for divorce from that in which they are placed in the ordinary courts of the land. This thing is proved to the hilt. We have the committee report. Why now in committee of the whole are we going to challenge it? In my opinion, there is no question about it that this divorce has been proved to the hilt.
