speechtext:
This afternoon some mention has been made of justice being done in this case. On the majority of previous occasions when we were dealing with previous bills and were asked to approve private bills for the relief of so and so, many of those cases were not contested. That would be an indication that at least to the parties concerned it was not a very serious matter whether the charges in the submission were proved or not because they were not interested in contesting the action in any case. That many of them could be contested, I think it is generally agreed. However, some of them are not contested.
This one was contested. It would therefore be an indication that the respondent in this particular case did not think that justice would be served by this case not being opposed. Fundamentally she has come to parliament and asked parliament to hear her side of the story and to give her relief which is exactly the opposite of the relief for which the petitioner is asking in this action.
If justice is to be done it means that there must be no doubt in the minds of members, or no reasonable doubt, that this matter is in order. But it is my contention in this case that there is a very great deal of wrong not only in respect of the submissions made by the many persons who participated in the case but in the circumstances surrounding the allegation of adultery. I believe that justice cannot be done while there is any doubt in anyone's mind that adultery was in fact committed and that it was proved to have been committed by the evidence submitted to the committee. I have looked up the definition of the word "adultery" in Webster's dictionary and it is very definite. It does not mean two people who know each other, or two people who have been exposed to certain circumstances or conditions. Adultery means sexual relationship between two people -a man and a woman-and in this case it does not seem to have been a probability. Therefore I suggest that justice cannot be done by granting a divorce.
We heard a number of witnesses, I believe seven at least, and they were in my opinion a motley crew. My colleague from Timmins has mentioned the length of time the investigators were working on the case, and it

Private Bill-Divorce
was certainly a lengthy period. The inference can therefore be drawn that the motive for taking such a long time was the monetary return which would accrue to these witnesses and also the fact that they could not find any evidence to establish adultery.
One of the investigators, Peter Rosen, makes his living at this kind of work and he came to the committee with so little use for justice that he told us he directed the operation on this particular night and instructed the people with him to break down the door of the house in question, which was locked. The house belonged to a lady and was a private residence but that night he instructed his colleagues to break the law by breaking down a door. One of the other witnesses said that he was scared of this sort of thing; he knew it was against the law and so he did not push very hard. Mr. Rosen, it appears, was not strong enough to bust down the door and that is the kind of evidence that we are asked to accept. Yet some hon. members will stand up in this chamber and say, "We want to see justice done." This man to whom I have referred has so little regard for the law and for justice that I believe in fact the only thing for which he had any regard was the payment for the type of evidence he procured.
A second man, Irving Gore, age 31, was also from Montreal and was a salesman by profession. This young man appeared to be a little too sharp and I suggest that he had other reasons for attending at this residence on the night in question. He said that he did not do this type of work normally but merely did so at the request of Mr. Rosen. He said he did not get paid for doing it but he was inconsistent in this respect because on other occasions apparently he had been paid for doing similar work. This man did not have too much initiative because he was directed to go to the back door and to watch it, I suppose having some knowledge that the front door was to be entered either by ringing the bell or by breaking down the door. He apparently did not try to turn the door knob on the back door and no one contradicted the witness who said that door was open and had not been locked at all. I therefore say that he went there on this occasion for personal reasons and not only because Mr. Rosen had invited him to do so, and in my opinion he was a very untrustworthy witness.
Then there were George and Don Kennedy. George Kennedy, age 31, was also a salesman, this time for one of our crown corporations. Frankly, I think we should be able to pay these people enough money that they do not have to traipse around doing this type of work, but I do think this fellow gave quite

reliable evidence, although the joke was made in committee that you have to be rather cautious about the people with whom you travel on T.C.A. because there may be investigators who have certain information from the other jobs on which they might be engaged. I think he was very indiscreet, to say the least, to participate in this type of work, particularly in respect of a divorce case such as the one with which we are dealing and which has already received so much publicity. However, George Kennedy was a comparatively reliable witness. He was under instructions and he got paid for this work, and therefore he was to report exactly what he had been told to investigate. He kept a record in a book of what he did and his testimony was very straightforward. He told us what was written in the book although I am not too sure that this was exactly what he saw.
Don Kennedy was an insurance investigator and I think most people who know investigators in this business have found that they do not normally work on such matters as this as a sideline. His evidence was very pat and had obviously been prepared as he would prepare a report on an investigation into an insurance adjustment matter or other work in his field. Nothing was left to chance-there was no danger of this witness ever being crossed up in respect of his investigation or evidence because he had been very sure to know exactly what he was talking about. This witness was also paid for the job he was hired to do and his evidence was directed towards one end, which in this case was divorce. The evidence of this man, probably more than anyone else's evidence, should be considered in the light of something we have heard in many contested divorce cases to the effect that one must always take with a grain of salt the evidence of a paid investigator.
On the other hand, there were three witnesses, Mr. Leslie Harvey Saunders, age 30, of Dorval, Quebec, who was an executive and a witness called on behalf of the petitioner- and I must apologize for not remembering that witness or his evidence, so I am not in a position to discuss it-next, Mr. George Rolland Foucher, who was an investigator. In respect of this man I would say that anyone who heard his evidence and only his evidence in committee could give any credence to the story he told, particularly in view of the manner in which he told it. I thought his manner of presentation was poorer than that of any other witness.
You are not doing too well yourself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The co-respondent in this case was not before the Senate but was before the

committee and the respondent herself appeared before the committee. In my opinion, her evidence substantiated her remarks. She gave straightforward evidence and yet her evidence was not so pat that you would think she had sat down and read it a few moments before but that she was thinking back to the time this allegation took place. The three sections which we think are violations of GATT directly are 37, 38 and 39. I was starting with 38 because I thought it was the most important section in regard to its relationship to GATT; that is, section 38(b), because section 38(b) in this bill is not limited to goods imported under such conditions as to cause or threaten injury to domestic producers. There is no qualification of that kind, and therefore this particular provision does not seem to us to be covered by article XIX of GATT. Surely there cannot be a much clearer violation of GATT than section 38(b) which says:
Where in any case or class of cases (b) the goods imported-
And then there is a whole list of conditions under which the goods would be imported, and it goes on to say that "the value for duty shall be determined in such manner as the minister prescribes." We would be very interested to see how the minister can relate that particular provision to our obligations under GATT.
We have not yet received from the minister in previous discussion of this bill any explanation about it; but whatever may be the intentions of the government in respect of the application of this section, we on this side can hardly accept a section that we think is a violation of GATT and therefore incompatible with Canadian interests. Perhaps the wording of this section does not

correspond with the intention of the government in regard to it. Perhaps we will find that out when we discuss the section.
The second section which we think is a violation of GATT is section 39 which, in our opinion, violates two provisions of GATT, namely article VII because of the use of the concept of cost of production plus a reasonable gross profit determined by the governor in council which, in our view, is equivalent to the fixing of arbitrary values. It also, in our view, violates article VI, paragraph 7 of GATT because a measure other than the anti-dumping duty is provided for the purpose of offsetting dumping in this particular section.
Now, whether section 39 is covered by the escape clause, which is article XIX of GATT, depends on the meaning of three words in the section, namely "material" and "may be". The section reads:
Where the minister is satisfied that material injury has been or may be caused to any industry in Canada,-
And so on. The GATT language is not injury that may be caused; the words used are "serious injury", and if material injury is not equivalent to serious injury or if "may be caused" is not equivalent to "threaten", which is the GATT language, section 39 is not covered by the escape clause and therefore it is a violation of GATT. If the minister had desired to be absolutely certain in this clause that GATT was not being violated, surely he should have used the language of GATT, he should have used the words "threaten serious injury".
The final section which we think violates GATT is section 37, which is new. When it is interpreted in the light of the very arbitrary and vague definition of cost of production and gross profit contained in section 35 and section 34, it appears to us clear that for all practical purposes the value for duty determined under this provision in section 37 will be arbitrary. Moreover, in section 37 no reference is made to actual or potential injury to domestic producers. Therefore, it follows that section 37 is contrary to article VII of GATT and that it is not even covered by the escape clause. It is a direct violation of an international agreement which we have accepted in the provisions of GATT.
These, Mr. Chairman, are the three clauses which we think do violate our undertakings under GATT. The minister may be able to remove our apprehensions in respect of one or possibly two, but on the wording of section 38(b) it is impossible for us to reconcile this in any way, shape or form with GATT.

"Cost of production" means an amount that in accordance with good business principles and practices fairly reflects the manufacture or production costs of the goods at the time of shipment to Canada.
What concerns me is this. Cost of production is something that I think I can understand and I can understand departmental officials seeking to ascertain what it is, but instead of this definition helping to clarify the matter it seems to me that it only confuses it and introduces new and, if I may say so, what appear to be irrelevant criteria. If it reflects production costs, from what does it reflect them and what other factors does it reflect as well as production costs?
It seems to me that this is a definition of an important phrase that is only confusing. Indeed, if one were so minded I think one could attempt to ridicule it but that is not my purpose at all. The point I wish to make is that instead of the definition clarifying or being helpful or laying down any criteria that would be useful in the understanding of this phrase it lays down in a way that is not understandable a definition that is utterly meaningless and permits the introduction, I respectfully suggest, of any criteria that any administrative officer

Customs Act
might wish to use. The idea that the cost of production merely reflects production costs is a pretty discouraging definition. I wonder whether the minister could clarify what was intended there and whether he would give some consideration to attempting to clarify the language used?

This afternoon the minister indicated how important that was because like goods these days are not very often like. When similar goods are used as a basis of comparison under this section the fair market value will not apply, I suggest, as it does at the present time and that instead, under this section, use will be made of the cost of production of the imported goods plus the percentage of gross profit made on similar goods.
I have here an illustration which will show how this rule could apply in practice. The minister may be able to remove-and I hope he will be able to do so-our worry on this score. I can see that in theory a case can be made for the application of that principle and that practice. It may have merit on the theoretical ground. But it seems to me that in practice, if there is a material difference between the cost of production of the goods imported and that of the so-called similar goods, then surely section 37 could not apply because the goods compared would not in fact be similar goods and new section

As I said this afternoon, you get your package of lima beans, for instance, and you have a 12-ounce package. The Americans use a 10-ounce package. Frankly, we do not think that section 39 is a violation of GATT at all. GATT has sufficient references to fair market value and ordinary course of trade procedures. Paragraph (b) of subsection 1 of section 36 of the bill refers to the ordinary course of trade. A man who is a manufacturer must have a certain amount of profit by way of return in addition to his actual costs. Section 39 requires that the value for duty be not less than that which obtains in the ordinary course of trade. The cost of production has a bearing on the general agreement and in a brief I have here it says that the final act stipulates that such duties shall not be levied unless the effect of the dumping is such as to cause or threaten material injury.
These conditions have been written into section 39 and are to apply before the cost of production basis may be used. Paragraphs 2 (a) and 2 (b) of article VII of GATT require that the actual value in the ordinary course of trade be taken as the criterion of value. Surely the ordinary cost of trade infers that a reasonable amount will be earned over the cost of production. Section 39 of the bill provides for the addition of an amount representing gross profit having regard to the gross profit generally earned in that particular trade or business in the country of export. If you turn to the interpretative notes of the general agreement you will find the following with respect to article VII:
The wording of subparagraph (a) and (b) permits a contracting party to assess duty uniformly either (1) on the basis of a particular exporter's prices of the imported merchandise, or (2) on the basis of the general price level of like merchandise.
Section 39 is intended merely to assess duty on the general price level of like merchandise and nothing more. This is interesting. At the review session of GATT in 1955 customs experts from all over the world, including some of our own, examined the cost of production clauses appearing in the legislation of several members of GATT, and there are cost of production clauses. Whatever they may have said verbally or whatever their thinking may have been, there was no reference in the report whatsoever to the inclusion of these cost of production clauses which have crept in between the former review and the one which took place in 1955.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-58, to amend the Canadian Citizenship Act.
She said: Mr. Speaker, in speaking on second reading of this bill I have a few general remarks to make. I think the bill with the explanatory notes pretty well stands on its own feet, but I have noticed certain remarks have been made about it and certain expressions of reservations have been voiced by members and others.
Subsection (1) of section 19 of the present act gives the governor in council power to revoke the citizenship of naturalized Canadians for the various reasons enumerated in that subsection. Briefly the grounds are that the person has: 1, assisted an enemy of Canada in time of war; 2, obtained his citizenship by false representation or fraud; 3, has resided outside of Canada for six years and has not maintained substantial connection with Canada; 4, has resided outside of Canada for two years in a country of which he was a citizen before he became a Canadian citizen and has not maintained substantial connection with Canada; 5, while out of Canada has shown disaffection or disloyalty to Her Majesty; or 6, has been convicted by a Canadian court of an offence involving disaffection or disloyalty to Her Majesty.
A natural-born Canadian citizen cannot lose his Canadian citizenship for any of these reasons and many naturalized Canadians and natural born Canadians as well feel very strongly that these provisions discriminate against the naturalized Canadian citizen and consequently the citizenship of a naturalized Canadian is sometimes referred to as being second class citizenship.
The amendment will repeal the existing subsection (1) of section 19 altogether, but it must be noted that under the amendment the naturalized Canadian citizen can still have his Canadian citizenship revoked by the governor in council if he is charged with a treasonable offence and, being abroad, fails to return to Canada and stand trial for that

offence. If such person does return to Canada and is convicted, he will suffer the punishment prescribed under the Criminal Code or the Official Secrets Act for the offence but he will not be subject to loss of citizenship.
An alien seeking Canadian citizenship must satisfy a court that he has the necessary qualifications required by the law for Canadian citizenship, which include such things as good character, an adequate knowledge of English or French, an adequate knowledge of the responsibility and privileges of Canadian citizenship. These qualifications are set out in section 10 of the act and it will be noted that the bill proposes amending paragraphs (f) of subsection (1) of section 10 to require the applicant to satisfy a court that he intends to comply with the oath of allegiance set forth in the second schedule.
Representations have been made to me since the first reading of this bill to the effect that the new proposed paragraph (c) of clause 19(1) might be misinterpreted. Provision, of course, is made for enquiry into any case under section 19(4) of the act. However, after serious consideration, I feel it is only proper to remove any doubt as to the intention of this bill, and therefore when we come to the appropriate section I shall ask one of my colleagues to move that this paragraph be deleted from the bill.
Under the existing act difficult questions of law and fact sometimes arise in relation to the question of whether a naturalized or natural born Canadian citizen has ceased to be a Canadian citizen. The bill provides machinery whereby these difficult cases can be referred to a court or a commission for study and a ruling. The act provides that any commission established under subsection (4) of section 19 must be presided over by a person who holds or has held high judicial office. So, therefore, whether the question is referred to a court or a commission the issue will be dealt with by a competent tribunal. This guarantees the naturalized Canadian a greater security in his new citizenship, and will encourage him in a fuller and more useful participation in Canadian life.

I think I heard the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) mention today that in 1945 a similar coincidence developed when a resolution for a bill of rights was introduced on the same day that the citizenship act was adopted. I rather pay some attention to this strange coincidence, and I should like to consider this matter from that standpoint and not at all from a party standpoint as it does not have any political significance whatever. I am confident that a matter of this kind will be considered purely on its merits by the house and by the minister who has all the sympathy necessary for considering citizenship in Canada.
Actually the premise of what I should like to say exists in the bill itself. The bill does classify citizens so far as losing their citizenship is concerned. The bill indicates that under certain conditions a naturalized citizen can lose his citizenship but no indication is given that for the same offences or under the same conditions a natural-born citizen will also lose his citizenship.
Let me illustrate what I mean. It is suggested that when a naturalized citizen commits the offence of treason or commits an offence against the Official Secrets Act he can lose his citizenship. A native born citizen can also commit treason and can also be found guilty of an offence against the Official Secrets Act. If a natural born citizen and a naturalized citizen both commit the offence of treason and are found guilty of the same offence I think the punishment should be the same for both.

Then the legislation should clearly state so. My submission is that it should apply to both who commit the same offence and fail to return to Canada. The natural born and the naturalized citizen should be treated in the same way and punished identically for having committed the same offence. I think my proposition is quite clear and simple and I do not think I am asking for anything that is not reasonable under the circumstances. I think the legislation should so provide. Otherwise, what are we doing? We are actually creating a cleavage between two classes of citizens. We are creating different rights for different types of citizens and that is not just a simple matter. I should like to point out that one of our provinces has made the difference even clearer. In the province of Quebec the election act adopted in 1952, I believe, has this provision:
When, upon application for the entry or for the striking off of names, the board of re visors comes to the conclusion that a person entered on an electoral list is not a Canadian citizen by birth, it may require such person to show by his certificate of naturalization or citizenship that he has the status of a Canadian citizen-
It is a perfectly proper provision in so far as having the right to vote is concerned, but here a difference is created between a citizen who is naturalized and one who is natural born. The naturalized citizen must produce his documents in order to be entered on the lists. A natural born citizen is not obliged to produce his documents. If the one is called upon to produce his naturalization papers, the other should be called upon to produce his birth certificate. Why should the one be believed and not the other? I am only citing this to show that if our citizenship law does create a difference the province has taken advantage of it and I think to the detriment of good law, good citizenship and equal rights.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) today spoke so feelingly and so passionately about the equal rights of citizens, I was reminded that this is the first time I have heard him emphasize equal rights for all citizens. I emphasize that to the

minister of immigration. This bill does not allow for equal rights to all citizens. It draws a line of demarcation. It may be a very thin line and the difference may be very subtle, but at the same time it is palpable.
I should like to draw the attention of the house to the fact that there are many painful memories which are still fresh in the minds of many people as a result of the fact that in some countries there was more than one class of citizenship. Certainly the history of the last 100 years should cause hon. members of this house to be horrified by the possibility of fostering in Canada, in even the subtlest form, two different classes of citizens. Whether or not we admit it, whether or not we like to admit it, I think if hon. members would look at the clauses of the bill they would find that there is that difference which I am pleading should be changed or eliminated. I have already given an illustration to show that if a similar offence were committed by both classes, the punishment should be identical.
I should like to point out also, Mr. Speaker, to hon. members that if we allow that difference to be created in one level of our law, other differences can also be created. For example, what is there to prevent parliament from adopting a bill to the effect that only natural born citizens shall be eligible for membership in Her Majesty's privy council? It is possible, by law, to say that only those who are born in this country shall qualify to serve in Her Majesty's privy council. We do not want that. If we adopt such a principle in one bill we do not know how it may work in another bill in the future.
If there are going to be two classes of citizens, one natural born and one naturalized, what is going to prevent parliament from enacting a law that only native born citizens can serve as judges in Her Majesty's courts or even be entitled to election to the House of Commons? I am very fearful of the possibilities that we are, by this bill, fostering. There now exists a difference in our citizenship. I shall, Mr. Speaker, when we are dealing with the bill in committee, move an amendment which the minister may consider. I appeal to all hon. members in the house to consider it because it is far beyond party lines. I should like to recommend it to the minister. I do not know whether I have permission to speak about it at this stage, but I shall not. I should like to make my appeal now to all hon. members to disregard party lines. I think this transcends all politics, all party lines, especially in view of the warm, genuine, sincere appeal made today by the Prime Minister, the Leader of the 57071-3-297J

I have here a newspaper article which I should like to read. It is an article that appeared in a newspaper published in Hamilton which I believe is the hon. lady's home

city. I should just like to read part of this article and to say that I concur in what is said. It reads as follows:
The Conservative government will soon bring the rights of "naturalized" Canadians into line with those of "natural-born" citizens.
Chief aim of the government is to eliminate the feeling among many new Canadians that "naturalized" citizenship is insecure-a feeling prompted by clauses of the Canadian Citizenship Act which appear to discriminate against the newcomer.
The act provides that the status of naturalized citizens-those born abroad and subsequently nationalized-is subject to review at any time by the government. It may cancel citizenship for reasons such as:
Residence abroad for six years without maintaining "substantial connection" with Canada.
It is rather ambiguous, Mr. Speaker, according to my understanding of its terms.
Conviction by a Canadian court of "any offence involving disaffection or disloyalty to Canada."
Showing oneself, while abroad, "by act or speech disaffected or disloyal to Her Majesty".
The natural born Canadian, on the other hand, can lose his citizenship only if he becomes a citizen of another country.
There is a vast difference in the two arrangements, as between Canadian born and natural-born citizens.
Acting Citizenship and Immigration Minister Davie Fulton said Tuesday he was impressed with the argument that the present act discriminates against the naturalized citizen.

In my opinion, this bill is an encroachment upon the rights of Canadian citizens of foreign origin who have come here to co-operate

with us, native Canadians, in the welfare of our fellow-citizens and in the development of our country. I am surprised at the stand taken by the minister in introducing such a bill, because we know that she has children, she is Canadian and, I admit, a model wife. Indeed, this bill will deny certain rights to our fellow-citizens who have come from other countries to join with us in the building of the Canadian nation.
As I said a moment ago, the Prime Minister put before us this morning a bill aiming at the protection of human rights and the prevention of any "discrimination" whatsoever.
This evening, as I said, we are asked to pass a bill which tends precisely to discriminate against a certain category of Canadians.
If we accept in this country that some fellow citizens who came from abroad to join us and add to the Canadian nation, we must consider them as Canadians, as our own people.
When a foreigner wants to establish himself in Canada, he has to put in an application. I realize that the Department of Citizenship and Immigration then proceeds to make a serious inquiry and that the applicant is admitted only if he is a desirable citizen, able to adapt himself to our Canadian way of life. Five years after he is admitted to Canada, a person of foreign origin declares his intention to become a Canadian citizen and during the following year, the minister may still make another inquiry in this case, which means that, following the investigations made before his admission to this country and during the six years he has resided here, we should be able to judge if such person could become a good Canadian citizen or should be returned to his home country.
Serious investigations were made in each case and in this connection, Mr. Speaker, I must say I have always wondered why it has been impossible for members, as well as for the persons concerned, to know why certain applications from immigrants wishing to take up residence in Canada were turned down.
I am one of those who believe that immigration is necessary in a country as large as ours. That is my personal opinion, but I do not believe that with a population of 17 million people, we can manage to make of our country what we would like it to become, if we do not let in the many immigrants who have decided to take up residence here. On the other hand, if we accept them, they must enjoy the same protection as that enjoyed by our natural bom citizens.
Canadian Citizenship Act

The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Is there any agreement between the federal government and city of Toronto requiring that lands of Fort York be maintained as a historic site?
2.	Has the federal government received from the city of Toronto a request for authority to use Fort York lands as a right of way?
3.	If so. has any decision been reached?
Answer by: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
1.	The letters patent dated 7th May, 1909 by which the crown in right of Canada transferred to the city of Toronto the lands of Fort York contain the following provision:
"To have and to hold the same unto the corporation, its successors and assigns, upon
and subject to the following trust and condition, namely; that the site of the old fort situate upon the said lands shall, as far as possible, be restored to its original condition, as shown on the attached copy of a plan of it, prepared by G. Nichols, government engineer, and dated Quebec, 24th June, 1816, and that the same shall be preserved and maintained in such conditions forever.
"Provided that upon the breach by the corporation, its successors and assigns of the trust and condition to which the grant hereby made is subject as aforesaid, such grant shall immediately become and be null and void, and it shall be lawful for us, our heirs, successors and assigns, in, to and upon the said lands hereby granted (or any part thereof in the name of the whole) to re-enter, and the same to have again, repossess, and enjoy as of our former estate therein anything herein contained to the contrary notwithstanding."
